prompt: At 6:30 p.m. Pacific time, a registered rep in Los Angeles starts cold-calling residential prospects in New York City. None of the prospects has an account with the firm or has given permission to be called. How should the branch manager view these calls?

options.text: They violate FINRA's rule, because it is 9:30 p.m. where the prospects live
They are permitted, because it is before 9 p.m. where the rep is calling from
They are permitted, provided each number was scrubbed against the national do-not-call list
They become violations once a prospect asks to be put on the firm's do-not-call list

explanation: FINRA Rule 3230 bars outbound telemarketing calls to a residence before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m., measured in the called party's local time. At 6:30 p.m. Pacific it is 9:30 p.m. Eastern, so these cold calls fall outside the window. With no existing relationship or prior permission, no exception applies, and do-not-call scrubbing does not cure a time-of-day violation.

distractorExplanations.b: Uses the caller's time zone; the 8 a.m.–9 p.m. window is measured at the called party's location, where it is already 9:30 p.m.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the do-not-call requirement with the time-of-day restriction; scrubbing the national registry does not make a 9:30 p.m. call permissible.
distractorExplanations.d: Mixes up two separate rules: a firm-specific do-not-call request governs future calls, but these calls already break the calling-hours limit.

prompt: A rep at a long-established broker-dealer is hosting a free retirement-planning seminar at a public library. She wrote a slide deck on general income strategies that names no specific fund or product, and she will hand printed copies to about 60 retail attendees. What does FINRA Rule 2210 require before she uses the deck?

options.text: No review, since seminar materials count as unscripted public appearances
A principal's review within 30 days after use, as with correspondence
Approval by a qualified registered principal before first use
Filing with FINRA at least 10 business days before the seminar date

explanation: Written material distributed or made available to more than 25 retail investors within 30 calendar days is a retail communication. Under Rule 2210, an appropriately qualified principal must approve a retail communication before the earlier of its use or filing. A general deck that promotes no investment company or other filing-trigger product does not need to be filed by an established firm, but pre-approval still applies. Her live, unscripted remarks are a public appearance, which is supervised but not pre-approved.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the rep's live, unscripted remarks (a public appearance) with the written slides, which are a retail communication requiring pre-approval.
distractorExplanations.b: Applies the correspondence standard; correspondence goes to 25 or fewer retail investors, and 60 attendees makes this a retail communication.
distractorExplanations.d: Pre-filing 10 business days ahead applies to a new member's first year and certain products, not a general deck at an established firm.

prompt: A rep wants the firm's public website to feature a short written quote from a long-time retail client praising the rep's portfolio reviews. The client was not paid anything for the quote. Which disclosure must the firm include with the testimonial?

That it may not reflect other clients' experience or future performance
That the client's account returns were verified by the firm's outside auditor
That FINRA reviewed the testimonial and found it fair and balanced

explanation: Rule 2210 lets a retail communication use a testimonial about the firm's investment advice or performance only with prominent disclosure that it may not be representative of other customers' experience and is no guarantee of future performance or success. A paid-testimonial statement is added when the client receives more than $100; an unpaid quote needs no compensation statement.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the paid-testimonial rule: a statement about compensation is required when the client is paid more than $100, not when unpaid.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a verification requirement; Rule 2210 requires disclosures about representativeness and future results, not an audit of returns.
distractorExplanations.d: Implying FINRA approval is itself misleading; FINRA does not approve communications, and the firm's principal performs the review.

Stop calling if the customer's number is also on the national registry
Stop sales calls for 18 months, then resume under the business relationship
Add the number to its firm-specific do-not-call list and stop sales calls

The firm may still contact the customer about servicing the account, just not to solicit.

prompt: A long-time FINRA member prepares a newspaper ad that says, "Our growth accounts rose sharply last year, so new clients should count on the same result." The ad names the firm and promotes that strategy. Which statement about the ad is correct?

options.text: It is prohibited because it implies that past performance will recur
It may run if a footnote says past performance does not guarantee future results
It is correspondence, because each newspaper reader sees the ad alone
It must be filed 10 business days before use because it cites last year's results

explanation: FINRA Rule 2210 forbids a communication that implies past performance will recur. Telling new clients to count on last year's result is that implication. A footnote disclaimer does not repair a headline that makes the promise. A newspaper ad offered to the public is a retail communication. Citing results does not, by itself, force an established firm to file the ad 10 business days before use.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats a disclaimer as a cure; the rule still bars a claim that last year's result is what new clients should expect.
distractorExplanations.c: Misclassifies the audience; a newspaper ad is made available to the public, far beyond 25 retail investors, so it is not correspondence.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a filing trigger; mentioning past results does not by itself require pre-use filing at an established firm.

prompt: At 11 a.m. in the prospect's own city, a rep dials a home number taken from a lead list the firm bought. The number is on the national do-not-call registry. The prospect has no account, has never inquired, and has given no written permission to be called. May the rep make this sales call?

options.text: Yes, because 11 a.m. local time is inside the 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. window for a cold call to a residence
No, because buying a lead list does not create an established business relationship
Yes, because a purchased list counts as the prospect's own inquiry within the past three months
Yes, if the rep states the firm name before describing the investment

explanation: FINRA Rule 3230 bars a sales call to a number on the national do-not-call registry unless the firm has an established business relationship, prior express written consent, or the caller has a personal relationship with the person. Paying for a lead list creates none of those. An 11 a.m. local time sits inside the 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. window for a cold call to a residence, but a permitted hour does not override the registry.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops at the time-of-day test; a call inside 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. is still barred when the national registry applies and no exception fits.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents an inquiry; that exception requires the person to have contacted the firm, not the firm to have purchased a list.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses identification with consent; stating the firm name does not create written permission or a business relationship.

prompt: A rep will give an unscripted talk, with no slides or handouts, at a weekend seminar open to the public. She plans to recommend shares of one listed company, and she holds a material long position in that company. What does FINRA require of the recommendation?

options.text: Word-for-word principal approval before she speaks, because every seminar is a retail communication
No added disclosure, because an unscripted talk sits outside Rule 2210
A reasonable basis, plus disclosure of that financial interest and its nature
Filing a transcript with FINRA at least 10 business days before the seminar

explanation: Unscripted seminar remarks are a public appearance, so the spoken words are not pre-approved the way a retail communication is. Rule 2210 still requires a reasonable basis before she recommends a security. She must also disclose a financial interest in the issuer that is more than nominal, including that it is a long position. Scripts and slides would be separate communications, and she is using neither.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a public appearance with a retail communication; unscripted remarks are supervised, not approved word for word in advance.
distractorExplanations.b: Drops the recommendation standard; a public appearance must still meet content standards, including a reasonable basis and conflict disclosure.
distractorExplanations.d: Applies a filing clock to spoken remarks; an unscripted talk is not submitted to FINRA 10 business days before she speaks.

prompt: A rep's cousin asked this firm to stop calling and was placed on the firm's own do-not-call list. The cousin's home number is also on the national registry. The rep wants to solicit the cousin at 2 p.m. local time and cites their family relationship. Which view is correct?

options.text: The call is allowed, because a family relationship overrides both the firm list and the national registry
The call is allowed, because 2 p.m. is inside the 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. window
The call is allowed once the cousin is deleted from the national registry only
The call is prohibited, because a firm-specific request has no relationship exception

explanation: Under FINRA Rule 3230, a personal relationship can permit a call to a number on the national do-not-call registry. It does not permit a call to someone who told that firm to stop. The firm-specific list has no exception for family, an existing account, or the hour of the call. A 2 p.m. local time would matter only if the call were otherwise allowed.

distractorExplanations.a: Overextends the personal-relationship exception, which can apply to the national registry and not to a stop request made to the firm.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses the calling-hours window as if it erased a do-not-call request; 2 p.m. does not authorize a call the person told the firm to stop.
distractorExplanations.c: Fixes the wrong list; removing the national registration would leave the firm's own do-not-call instruction in place.

prompt: A retail brochure compares the firm's bond ladder with a bank certificate of deposit and quotes only the ladder's higher yield. It never says the bonds can fall in value and are not bank deposits, while the certificate is a deposit product. What does FINRA Rule 2210 require in this comparison?

options.text: Disclosure of material differences, including safety and fluctuation of principal
No added disclosure, because the higher yield alone lets a reader compare the two products
A filing at least 10 business days before use, because every comparison must be pre-filed
Deletion of the yield, because a retail brochure may not mention income at all

explanation: Rule 2210 requires a retail comparison of investments or services to disclose all material differences, including safety, guarantees or insurance, and fluctuation of principal or return where those differences apply. Quoting only a higher yield leaves out that the bond ladder can lose value and is not a bank deposit. A general comparison at an established firm is not automatically a filing due 10 business days before use.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats yield as the only difference; the rule requires material differences such as safety and principal fluctuation to be disclosed.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a filing category; a general product comparison is not one of the retail pieces that must be filed 10 business days before use.
distractorExplanations.d: Bans a fact the rule allows; the brochure may discuss yield when the comparison stays fair and the material differences are disclosed.

prompt: Six weeks after its FINRA membership became effective, a broker-dealer wants to launch a public website describing brokerage services for retail investors. The pages promote those services and name the account types offered. What must the firm do before the site goes live?

options.text: Have a principal approve it after posting, because a website is correspondence
Get principal approval and file it at least 10 business days before first use
File it within 10 business days after launch, as with an established firm's fund ad
Skip both approval and filing, because the site is the firm's own property

explanation: For one year after FINRA membership becomes effective, a new member must file retail communications used in public media, including a generally accessible website, at least 10 business days before first use. An appropriately qualified principal must approve that retail communication before the earlier of its use or filing. Filing within 10 business days after use is a different clock, used for certain product ads such as a specific mutual fund outside the new-member year.

distractorExplanations.a: Misclassifies a public website; content promoting the firm's services to the public is a retail communication, not correspondence reviewed after the fact.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses the after-launch filing clock; during the first year a new member's public website is filed at least 10 business days before first use.
distractorExplanations.d: Drops both duties; promotional website content still needs principal approval and, in the first year, pre-use filing.

prompt: A rep places an allowed cold call to a residence at 4 p.m. in the city of the person called. The number is on neither the national registry nor the firm's own do-not-call list. Which facts must the rep give on that call?

options.text: Only the firm's name, with any other details mailed later if the person asks
That FINRA's advertising staff reviewed and cleared the call script
The caller's name, the firm's name, a contact address or phone number, and that the call is a solicitation
No identification until the person agrees to hear a pitch, because those facts are required only after a purchase

explanation: On an outbound telemarketing call, FINRA Rule 3230 requires the caller to give the caller's name, the member's name, an address or telephone number at which the member can be contacted, and that the purpose is to solicit the purchase of securities or a related service. This call at 4 p.m. local time is inside the 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. window, and the number is not on a do-not-call list, but those facts do not remove the identification duty.

distractorExplanations.a: Cuts the required introduction down to the firm name; the rule also requires the caller's name, a contact address or number, and the sales purpose.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents a FINRA clearance; FINRA does not pre-clear ordinary cold-call scripts, and implying that review would be misleading.
distractorExplanations.d: Delays identification until after a sale; the caller must provide the name, firm, contact, and purpose on the solicitation call itself.

prompt: A branch repeats one lunch seminar on three weekdays. Each day, 10 retail guests receive the same printed sheet recommending a sector ETF. All 30 guests receive that sheet inside one 30-calendar-day period. How should the firm classify the sheet?

options.text: Correspondence, because each lunch has only 10 guests and never crosses 25 investors
A public appearance, so the sheet is supervised like the talk and needs no pre-approval
An institutional communication, because a hosted lunch is not a retail distribution
A retail communication, so a principal must approve it before first use

explanation: Rule 2210 counts a written piece as a retail communication when it is distributed to more than 25 retail investors within any 30-calendar-day period. The same sheet reaches 30 retail guests in that window, even though each lunch has only 10. An appropriately qualified principal must approve it before first use. The spoken remarks can be a public appearance; the handout is classified on its own audience.

distractorExplanations.a: Splits one distribution by room; the rule adds up retail investors who receive the same piece within 30 calendar days, and 30 is more than 25.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the handout with the talk; slides, scripts, and handouts used at a seminar are communications classified by who receives them.
distractorExplanations.c: Misreads the audience; the guests are retail investors, so the sheet is not an institutional communication.

prompt: Four months ago a person called the firm to ask about municipal bonds, then never opened an account or traded. That home number is on the national do-not-call registry and not on the firm's own list. A rep wants to solicit the person at noon in that person's city. May the rep call?

options.text: Yes. Any inbound question creates an 18-month established business relationship
Yes. Noon local time is inside the 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. cold-call window, so the registry does not apply
Yes. Asking about bonds is itself a securities transaction with the firm
No. An inquiry supports calls for three months, and four months have passed

explanation: An established business relationship based only on an inquiry lasts three months after the person contacted the firm about a product or service. At four months, that exception to the national do-not-call registry has ended. The 18-month window applies after a financial transaction, a securities position, a money balance, or account activity, and none of those occurred. Noon is inside the 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. cold-call window, which does not override the registry.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses the transaction window; an inquiry alone supports calls for three months, not 18 months.
distractorExplanations.b: Answers only the time-of-day question; a noon call is still barred by the national registry once the three-month inquiry window has closed.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a question as a trade; an inquiry is not a financial transaction, a securities position, or account activity.

prompt: A U.S. citizen applying for a new individual brokerage account gives only a P.O. box as his address and says he prefers not to share where he lives. He supplies his name, date of birth, and Social Security number. Under the firm's Customer Identification Program, what should the rep do?

options.text: Accept the P.O. box, since any valid mailing address meets CIP standards
Accept the P.O. box once his Social Security number has been verified
Obtain a residential or business street address before opening the account
Open the account and file a SAR, since withholding an address is suspicious

explanation: CIP rules under the USA PATRIOT Act require the firm to obtain, before opening an account, an individual's name, date of birth, address, and identification number. For an individual, the address must be a residential or business street address; a P.O. box works only as a mailing address. The firm then verifies identity within a reasonable time and should not open the account if required information is withheld.

distractorExplanations.a: Ignores the street-address requirement; a P.O. box can be a mailing address, but CIP needs a residential or business street address.
distractorExplanations.b: Verifying the SSN satisfies a different CIP data element; it does not replace the required residential or business street address.
distractorExplanations.d: Jumps to a SAR; the first step is obtaining the missing CIP element, and a SAR depends on facts suggesting suspicious activity, not one gap.

The company's most recent audited balance sheet and income statement

prompt: An 81-year-old customer asks to wire $90,000 to an overseas "friend" she met online. Suspecting financial exploitation, the firm places a temporary hold on the disbursement under FINRA Rule 2165. What notice must the firm give after placing the hold?

Notify the customer's adult children, whether or not they are on the account
Notify the overseas recipient that the wire is under internal review
Within 2 business days, notify authorized parties and the trusted contact

explanation: Rule 2165 lets a firm delay a disbursement or transaction for a specified adult (65 or older, or 18+ with a qualifying impairment) when it reasonably believes exploitation is occurring. prompt: A customer calls her rep: "Buy 500 shares of XYZ for me sometime today; you decide the exact time and price." The account has no written discretionary authorization. How may the rep handle the order?

options.text: Accept it; time-and-price discretion for the day needs no written authority
Decline it until the customer signs a written discretionary authorization
Accept it, and switch to a similar stock if XYZ looks weak later in the day
Accept it as a good-till-canceled order that stays open until she revokes it

No written authorization is needed, but time-and-price discretion is limited to the day it is granted unless the customer gives a signed, dated written instruction otherwise. Choosing the security, quantity, or action would require written discretionary authority.

Never, since the ODD replaces the agreement
Before the account is approved
Within 30 days after the first options trade

explanation: Under FINRA Rule 2360, the customer must receive the ODD at or before account approval. The signed options agreement must be returned within 15 days after approval, or the customer may only close existing positions.

distractorExplanations.b: Delivering the ODD does not replace the signed agreement, which must arrive within 15 days of approval.
distractorExplanations.c: The ODD is required before approval, but the signed options agreement may follow within 15 days after approval.
distractorExplanations.d: The deadline is tied to account approval, not the first trade, and it is 15 days.

prompt: Elena and Marco hold a cash brokerage account as joint tenants with right of survivorship. Marco is traveling, and Elena phones an order to sell 200 shares of a listed stock they bought together. Neither owner has died. What may the representative do?

options.text: Accept Elena's sell order without Marco on the line
Wait until Marco returns and repeats the sell order on a recorded line
Ask Marco to sign a limited power of attorney before Elena may sell the joint shares
Refuse the sale, because a survivorship account is frozen whenever one owner is traveling

explanation: Each joint tenant with right of survivorship may enter orders while both owners are alive, so Elena's sale of the 200 shares does not need Marco on the phone. Survivorship matters at death; it does not freeze the account because an owner is traveling. A check for the proceeds would still be payable to both names, but the order itself is one either owner may place.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a joint registration with a two-signature trade; either JTWROS owner may enter an order, so Marco does not have to repeat it.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a co-owner as a third party; Elena already has trading authority on the joint account and does not need a power of attorney from Marco.
distractorExplanations.d: Applies the death freeze to ordinary travel; the account is restricted when an owner dies, not when one owner is away.

prompt: A client signed a limited trading authorization yesterday so her representative may choose stocks without calling her. No principal has accepted that discretionary account in writing. This morning the representative wants to buy 150 shares of a listed industrial company. What is the correct step?

options.text: Enter the 150-share purchase now, since her signature alone turns on discretion the next morning
Wait until a principal accepts the account in writing
Enter the purchase and have a principal initial the order ticket sometime next week
Label the ticket not-held so the representative may choose the stock without principal acceptance

explanation: FINRA Rule 3260 permits discretion only after the customer has given prior written authorization and a principal has accepted the account in writing. The signed form is already in the file, but the 150-share purchase still waits for that acceptance. Once the account is accepted, each discretionary order is marked and reviewed promptly by a principal.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops at the customer's signature; Rule 3260 also requires a principal's written acceptance of the account before any discretionary order is entered.
distractorExplanations.c: Delays principal acceptance until after the trade and past a prompt review; the account must be accepted in writing before discretion is used.
distractorExplanations.d: Misuses a not-held ticket; not-held instructions cover time and price only, and choosing the security is still discretion.

prompt: Priya, age 44, is opening an individual cash account. After the representative explains the request, she declines to name a trusted contact. Her name, residential street address, date of birth, and Social Security number are already on the application. May the firm open the account?

options.text: No. Keep the account closed until she names a trusted contact, which is a required identity item
No. The request was improper because trusted contacts are collected only from senior customers
Yes. Record that she was asked and declined, then open the account
Yes, but only if a spouse is added as joint owner to stand in for the missing contact

explanation: FINRA Rule 4512 requires reasonable efforts to obtain a trusted contact on a non-institutional account. Priya is 44, and the request still applies; it is not limited to seniors. Her refusal does not block opening once the firm asked and documented the decline. A trusted contact is not an owner and is not replaced by adding a joint tenant.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns a reasonable-efforts request into a hard condition; Rule 4512 lets the customer decline, and the cash account may still be opened.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the trusted-contact request with the age test for a Rule 2165 hold; firms ask retail customers generally, including a customer who is 44.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes a joint owner for a contact person; declining to name a trusted contact does not require a second name on the registration.

prompt: A new individual account applicant provides his name, residential street address, date of birth, and tax identification number. He describes his work only as self-employed and will not say whether he is associated with a broker-dealer. Which addition does the new-account record still need?

options.text: No further item, because the street address and tax number already finish the identification record
A principal-signed balance sheet for his business before this cash account may be approved
A trusted contact's name and phone number, treated as mandatory in the same way as his tax number
Employer details and any association with a member firm

explanation: For a natural person, FINRA Rule 4512 requires reasonable efforts, before the initial transaction settles, to obtain the occupation, the employer's name and address, and whether the customer is associated with another member. Calling himself self-employed does not supply the business name and address or the associated-person answer. That association answer is what starts the prior-consent process if he works at another member.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the CIP identity file as the whole new-account record; employer details and member-firm association are separate elements he has not given.
distractorExplanations.b: Demands a financial statement this cash-account record does not require; the gaps are employer identity and associated-person status.
distractorExplanations.c: Makes the trusted contact mandatory like his tax number; the firm must ask for a trusted contact, and the customer may decline, which is not the employer and association information still missing.

prompt: A grandmother wants to give 80 shares of listed stock to her grandson, age 9, under UGMA. She also wants her own name on the account as joint owner so she can take the shares back if he skips college. How should the firm title the account?

options.text: A custodial UGMA account owned by the grandson
A joint account in both names so the grandmother can withdraw the shares if college is skipped
A revocable trust that sends the shares back to her if the grandson does not attend college
Her personal account, with a file note that the 80 shares are set aside for the grandson

explanation: An UGMA registration is a custodial account for one minor. The grandson, age 9, owns the 80 shares, and the gift is irrevocable, so the grandmother cannot keep a joint interest or a right to reclaim them if he skips college. One adult serves as custodian. She may be that custodian, but the shares are his.

distractorExplanations.b: Builds a joint account with a minor and a take-back right; UGMA has one minor owner, and the donor cannot withdraw the gift later.
distractorExplanations.c: Keeps a revocation path the gift statute does not allow; an UGMA transfer is irrevocable and is not a revocable trust.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaves the 80 shares in the donor's own account; a file note is not a completed gift, and the grandson never becomes the owner.

prompt: The president of Northline Tools Inc. asks the firm to open a margin account for the company in his personal name and Social Security number, so he can move cash without waiting for a board meeting. He says the charter allows the company to invest in securities. What should the firm require instead?

options.text: His personal guarantee and the company's latest audited income statement, instead of corporate papers
An account in the company's name and tax ID, with a trading resolution
A custodial account naming him as custodian for the company until the next board meeting
A numbered personal account, plus a memo that the cash is meant for Northline Tools

explanation: Company assets belong in an account opened in the corporation's name and tax identification number. A corporate resolution names the people who may enter orders, which is what he was trying to skip. His Social Security number would make the account his. A charter clause that allows investing is not margin-borrowing authority; that borrowing power still has to appear in the charter or bylaws.

distractorExplanations.a: Offers a guarantee and financial statements; neither document titles the account in the corporation's name or names who may trade.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses a minor's custodial form for a company; a corporation needs its own registration and a resolution, not a custodian.
distractorExplanations.d: Hides a personal registration behind a memo; the owner of record would still be the president, not Northline Tools.

prompt: Jonah and Denise hold a JTWROS cash account. Jonah sells 300 shares and asks for the proceeds check in his name only, because he was the one who called in the order. Denise is alive and has not signed any payment instruction. How should the check be drawn?

options.text: To Jonah alone, because the owner who enters the sale decides who is paid
To Jonah alone, because the first name on a joint registration is the payee
Payable to Jonah and Denise together
To Jonah alone after a principal approves the ticket, since that approval can drop a co-owner from the payee line

explanation: Jonah may enter the sale of the 300 shares, because either joint tenant can trade. A check is different. While both owners are alive and have not given written payment instructions, a distribution from the joint account is payable to both Jonah and Denise. Survivorship does not reassign the proceeds of an ordinary sale.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses trading authority with the payee on a check; either owner may sell, but the check still names every living joint owner.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats the order of names on the title as a payee ranking; JTWROS gives both owners a claim to the distribution.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses principal approval to rewrite ownership; a principal reviews the order and does not remove Denise from the check.

prompt: At 9:40 a.m. a customer tells her representative, "Use about $8,000 to buy a bank stock today. You choose the company and the price." There is no written discretionary authorization on the account. What may the representative do?

options.text: Buy a bank stock today, treating the choice of company as time-and-price discretion
Place a good-till-canceled not-held order and pick the bank on a later day
Enter the trade and mark the phone call as verbal discretion for a same-day pick
Refuse to choose the company without written discretion

explanation: Time-and-price discretion exists only after the customer names the security, the action, and the amount. This customer left the company open and capped the buy around $8,000, so the representative would be choosing the asset. That requires prior written discretionary authorization. A same-morning verbal instruction does not supply it, and the order cannot be carried into a later day.

distractorExplanations.a: Mislabels the choice of company as time and price; that limited authority exists only when the customer has already named the security.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaves the order open past today and still lets the representative pick the bank; written discretion is missing, and an oral time-and-price instruction would end the same day.
distractorExplanations.c: Relies on a verbal okay noted on the ticket; discretion over which security to buy has to be in a signed authorization first.

prompt: A new cash-account customer refuses to state his income, net worth, or investment experience. He then asks the firm to buy 100 shares of a listed company he names himself. The representative has made no recommendation. What may the firm do?

options.text: Open the account and accept his unsolicited order
Open it only after typing a moderate objective into the profile so the file looks finished
Refuse the account until income and net worth are collected as required identity items
Buy the shares in the representative's account and journal them over after he discloses finances

explanation: The firm must try to obtain an investment profile before it recommends a security or strategy. The customer may still decline to give income, net worth, or experience, and the account can be opened. He named the 100-share purchase himself, so the order is unsolicited and may be taken. The representative should not recommend anything on a blank profile, and the file should show what was refused.

distractorExplanations.b: Fabricates an objective the customer never gave; the record should show the refusal, not a made-up moderate profile.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats income and net worth as CIP identity fields; those figures are for recommendations, not a condition of an unsolicited cash order.
distractorExplanations.d: Moves the 100-share buy into the representative's own account; parking a customer trade there is not a substitute for a thin profile.

prompt: Helen, age 76, listed her nephew as the trusted contact on her individual account. The nephew calls and tells the representative to sell her entire equity-fund position today because he fears someone is pressuring her. He holds no power of attorney. What may the representative do?

options.text: Enter the sale, because a trusted contact automatically has authority to liquidate the account
Reject the nephew's order and escalate the concern
Enter the sale once the nephew is added as a joint owner before today's close
Sell the shares and send the cash to the nephew while the firm looks into the pressure

explanation: A trusted contact is a person the firm may call about possible financial exploitation, about how to reach Helen, or about whether a guardian or attorney-in-fact exists. Helen is 76, which makes a senior-exploitation review relevant, but the nephew's designation does not let him sell the fund. The representative refuses the order, writes up the call, and follows the firm's escalation steps.

distractorExplanations.a: Invents trading authority for a trusted contact; the designation lets the firm make inquiries, and it does not make the nephew an agent on a 76-year-old's account.
distractorExplanations.c: Turns a contact person into an owner during the call; joint registration would require Helen's own agreement and new account documents.
distractorExplanations.d: Sends her sale proceeds to someone who cannot transact; a trusted contact does not receive distributions from the account.

prompt: An UTMA account holds 120 shares for a minor who is 14. The child's uncle was the donor, and the child's aunt is the custodian. The uncle calls to sell the shares because he has changed his mind about the gift. The aunt has given no instruction. Who may direct a sale?

options.text: The uncle, because a donor may revoke the gift at any time before custodianship ends
The minor, because a 14-year-old may direct sales in an account opened for him
Only the aunt, and only if she decides a sale is appropriate
Either the uncle or the aunt, since both adults share authority over the custodial shares

explanation: The minor, age 14, owns the 120 shares, but only the custodian may enter orders. The aunt is the custodian, so the uncle's change of mind does not authorize a sale, and an UTMA gift cannot be revoked by the donor. The aunt may sell if she concludes the sale benefits the child; she is not required to follow the uncle.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives the donor a take-back power; an UTMA gift is irrevocable, and the uncle is not the custodian who can enter the sale.
distractorExplanations.b: Lets the 14-year-old trade the custodial account; he is the owner, but orders come from the custodian rather than from the minor.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the donor as a co-manager; only the named custodian, the aunt, has authority to direct a sale of the shares.

prompt: ABC Corp. announces a rights offering in which 4 rights plus $34 buy one new share. The stock still trades cum rights at $40. A customer holding 400 shares asks what each right is theoretically worth today. What is the theoretical value of one right?
explanation: While the stock trades cum rights, its price still includes the right, so value = (market price - subscription price) ÷ (rights per new share + 1) = (40 - 34) ÷ (4 + 1) = 6 ÷ 5 = $1.20. After the ex-rights date the +1 drops out: (ex-rights price - subscription price) ÷ rights per share.

distractorExplanations.b: Uses the ex-rights formula, (40 - 34) ÷ 4, on a cum-rights price; while the stock trades with the right attached, divide by N + 1.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the full $6 discount on one new share, but it takes 4 rights to buy that share, so the discount is spread across the rights.
distractorExplanations.d: Divides the market price by the rights ratio (40 ÷ 4); a right is worth only the discount below market, not a slice of the share price.

prompt: The same city has two new issues outstanding. One financed a parking garage and is payable solely from parking fees; the other financed an elementary school and is secured by the city's unlimited ad valorem taxing power. A customer asks how the two differ. Which comparison is accurate?

options.text: The school bond is a GO bond backed by taxes; the garage bond is a revenue bond paid from fees
The garage bond is a GO bond backed by fees; the school bond is a revenue bond paid from taxes
Both are GO bonds because the same city issued them and its taxing power backs each one
The school bond needs a feasibility study to issue; the garage bond needs voter approval to issue

explanation: A general obligation bond is backed by the issuer's full faith and credit, meaning its power to levy ad valorem (property) taxes, and usually needs voter approval. A revenue bond is paid only from the financed facility's revenues, such as parking fees, and is judged on a feasibility study and debt service coverage rather than voter approval.

distractorExplanations.b: Swaps the labels; a bond paid solely from user fees is a revenue bond, and a bond secured by unlimited taxing power is a GO bond.
distractorExplanations.c: The bond type depends on the pledged source of payment, not the issuer; one city can sell both GO bonds and revenue bonds.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the process: GO bonds usually need voter approval, while revenue bonds rely on a feasibility study of the facility's revenues.

prompt: With XYZ at $50, a customer buys 1 XYZ Mar 50 call at 3 and 1 XYZ Mar 50 put at 2. At expiration, at which XYZ prices does the position break even?
explanation: A long straddle has two breakevens because either leg can pay off, but only one leg finishes in the money, so that leg must recover the total premium. Total premium = 3 + 2 = 5. Upside: 50 + 5 = 55. Downside: 50 - 5 = 45. Max loss is $500 if XYZ closes exactly at 50.

distractorExplanations.a: Doubles the combined premium; each breakeven is the strike plus or minus the total premium of 5 points, not 10.
distractorExplanations.c: Splits the 5-point premium between the two sides; whichever leg finishes in the money must recover the full 5 points by itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses each leg's own premium (50 + 3 and 50 - 2); only one leg can be in the money, so it must recover both premiums.

prompt: A customer buys a 6% corporate bond at 108. It matures in 15 years and is callable at par in 5 years. Ranked from highest to lowest, how do its yields compare?

options.text: Yield to call, yield to maturity, current yield, nominal yield
Nominal and current yield tie at 6%, then yield to maturity, then yield to call
Nominal yield, current yield, yield to call, yield to maturity
Nominal yield, current yield, yield to maturity, yield to call

explanation: Buying above par means the 8-point premium is lost by redemption. Current yield = $60 ÷ $1,080 = 5.56%, below the 6% nominal. YTM spreads the premium loss over 15 years; YTC squeezes it into 5 years, so YTC is lowest. For a premium callable bond the rep must quote the lower yield to worst, here the yield to call.

distractorExplanations.a: That is the discount-bond order; when a bond is bought below par each yield beyond nominal rises, but this bond was bought above par.
distractorExplanations.b: Current yield uses the market price: $60 ÷ $1,080 = 5.56%, so it falls below the 6% nominal yield whenever the price is above par.
distractorExplanations.c: Swaps YTM and YTC; the premium is amortized over 5 years to the call versus 15 years to maturity, so YTC is the lower of the two.

prompt: A customer must pay a fixed $50,000 obligation in exactly 10 years. She wants to lock in her return today with no reinvestment risk and will hold the position in her traditional IRA. Which Treasury security best fits?

options.text: Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities maturing in 10 years
Treasury STRIPS maturing in 10 years
10-year Treasury notes paying semiannual interest
26-week Treasury bills rolled over at each maturity

explanation: STRIPS are zero-coupon Treasury principal or interest components bought at a discount and paid at face value at maturity. With no coupons to reinvest, the yield is locked in at purchase. Holding them in an IRA also avoids the annual phantom-income tax on accreted discount that a taxable account would owe.

distractorExplanations.a: TIPS adjust principal for CPI and pay semiannual interest, so coupons must be reinvested and the final dollar amount is not known in advance.
distractorExplanations.c: Semiannual coupons must be reinvested at future rates, which is exactly the reinvestment risk the customer wants to avoid.
distractorExplanations.d: Rolling bills exposes every rollover to whatever rates prevail at that time; it maximizes reinvestment risk rather than removing it.

prompt: With DEF at $42, a customer writes 1 uncovered DEF Jun 40 put at 3. What are her maximum potential gain and maximum potential loss on the position?

options.text: Max gain $300; max loss $3,700
Max gain $300; max loss $4,000
Max gain $3,700; max loss $300
Max gain $300; max loss unlimited

explanation: A put writer keeps the $300 premium if DEF stays at or above 40. The worst case is DEF going to zero: she must buy worthless stock at $40, losing $4,000, offset by the $300 premium. Max loss = (40 - 3) × 100 = $3,700, and breakeven is 37.

distractorExplanations.b: Ignores the $300 premium received; the premium reduces the loss if DEF falls to zero, so the loss is $4,000 - $300 = $3,700.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the roles; $300 is the most the writer can gain, and $3,700 is the writer's worst-case loss, not a potential gain.
distractorExplanations.d: Unlimited loss belongs to an uncovered call writer; a stock cannot fall below zero, so a short put's loss is capped at strike minus premium.

$500 gain

prompt: Mortgage rates fall sharply and refinancings surge in a CMO's collateral pool. A customer's tranche, sold with an expected average life of 9 years, now projects an average life of 3 years. Which tranche did she most likely buy?

options.text: A planned amortization class (PAC) tranche
A targeted amortization class (TAC) tranche
An accrual (Z) tranche paid after the earlier classes retire
A companion (support) tranche

explanation: Companion tranches exist to absorb prepayment variability so PAC holders get a predictable schedule. When refinancings surge, excess principal is paid to the companion first, so its average life shortens sharply and the holder reinvests at lower rates. Companions carry the most prepayment and extension risk, which is why they offer the highest yields.

distractorExplanations.a: PACs carry the most protection; principal follows a set schedule within a prepayment band, and the excess is shifted to companion classes.
distractorExplanations.b: TACs are protected against faster prepayments, with the excess shifted to companions; a sharp shortening points to the support class.
distractorExplanations.c: The Z-tranche accrues interest and receives principal only after earlier classes retire, so faster prepayments reach it last, not first.

prompt: A customer buys 1 JKL Oct 45 call at 5 and sells 1 JKL Oct 50 call at 2 in the same account. What are the position's maximum gain, maximum loss, and breakeven at expiration?

Max gain $200; max loss $300; breakeven $48
Max gain $300; max loss $200; breakeven $48
Max gain unlimited; max loss $300; breakeven $48

explanation: This is a debit call (bull) spread. Net debit = 5 - 2 = 3, which is the max loss ($300) if JKL ends at or below 45. Max gain = strike difference - debit = (50 - 45) - 3 = 2, or $200, at or above 50. Breakeven = lower strike + net debit = 45 + 3 = 48.

distractorExplanations.a: Subtracts the debit from the higher strike; call-spread breakeven is the lower strike plus the net premium, 45 + 3 = 48.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses gain and loss; the $300 net debit is what she can lose, and the 2 points left of the 5-point spread are what she can gain.
distractorExplanations.d: Ignores the short 50 call, which caps the upside; above 50 any further gain on the long call is offset by the short call.

prompt: A customer in the 32% federal tax bracket is offered an in-state municipal GO bond yielding 4.08%. Considering federal tax only, what yield would a fully taxable corporate bond need to match it?
explanation: Tax-equivalent yield = municipal yield ÷ (1 - tax bracket) = 4.08% ÷ (1 - 0.32) = 4.08% ÷ 0.68 = 6.00%. A taxable bond must yield 6.00% for the customer to keep the same 4.08% after federal income tax.

distractorExplanations.a: Multiplies by (1 - 0.32); that converts a taxable yield into its after-tax yield, which runs the formula backwards for a muni.

distractorExplanations.c: Counts 320 shares but keeps the old $140 basis, which would raise total basis from $11,200 to $44,800. A split does not increase total cost.
distractorExplanations.d: Multiplies the $140 price by 4 and gets $560, the reverse of the adjustment. The per-share basis falls to $35 while the count rises to 320.

prompt: Cumulative preferred with a $100 par states a $6 annual dividend. The issuer paid none of that dividend in the prior 2 years. It will now pay every preferred dividend currently due, including this year's $6, before common shareholders receive anything. How much is due on each preferred share?

options.text: $6 per share
$12 per share
$18 per share
$24 per preferred share

explanation: Cumulative preferred must be brought current before common is paid. Two missed years are 2 × $6 = $12 of arrears, and this year's dividend adds another $6, so 3 × $6 = $18 is due on each share. The $100 par names the stock; it is not multiplied into the dividend.

distractorExplanations.a: Pays only the current $6 and drops the arrears. On cumulative preferred, the two skipped years stay due and are paid together with this year's $6.
distractorExplanations.b: Stops at the arrears: 2 × $6 = $12. The stem includes this year's $6 as well, so the amount due before common is paid is $18.
distractorExplanations.d: Computes 4 × $6 = $24, one year too many. Only two years were skipped, plus the current year, which is three payments of $6.

prompt: The board declared a stock dividend equal to 50% of the common stock's value. The record date is Monday, March 9, and the payable date is Friday, March 20. A customer who buys and sells regular way asks when those shares go ex-distribution. Which day is the ex-date?

options.text: Monday, March 9, the record date
Friday, March 6
Friday, March 20
Monday, March 23

explanation: A stock dividend of 25% or more of the security's value goes ex-distribution on the first business day after the payable date. This one is 50% of value, and the payable date is Friday, March 20, so the ex-date is Monday, March 23. The common-stock trade itself still settles regular way on the next business day, T+1. The later ex-date decides who delivers the new shares.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses the ordinary cash-dividend timing, where a business-day record date is the ex-date. That rule is for distributions under 25% of value. This 50% stock dividend is dated from the payable date.
distractorExplanations.b: Picks the business day before the record date, Friday, March 6. That is neither the cash-dividend ex-date under T+1 nor the ex-date for a distribution of 25% or more.
distractorExplanations.c: Names the payable date itself, Friday, March 20. The ex-date is the next business day, Monday, March 23, after the new shares have been paid.

prompt: A shareholder already owns 1,200 common shares, and the company issues 1 right for each of them. She may buy 1 new share for 5 rights plus $25. She wants every new share those rights will buy. What does she have to turn in?

options.text: 1,200 rights and $6,000
240 rights and $6,000
1,200 rights and $30,000
5 rights and $25 for the whole position

explanation: She holds 1,200 rights, and each new share takes 5 of them, so 1,200 / 5 = 240 new shares. Cash due is 240 × $25 = $6,000. She delivers the full 1,200 rights together with that $6,000.

distractorExplanations.b: Uses 240 as the number of rights. That figure is the number of new shares, 1,200 / 5. The rights she turns in are all 1,200, along with $6,000.
distractorExplanations.c: Multiplies every one of the 1,200 rights by the $25 price and gets $30,000. The $25 is charged once per new share, and the rights buy only 240 shares.
distractorExplanations.d: States the terms for a single new share, 5 rights plus $25. She asked to use every right, which buys 240 shares for $6,000.

prompt: Dollar-priced sponsored ADRs appeal to a customer who wants shares of a French company without opening an overseas brokerage account. The receipts trade in dollars on a U.S. exchange. Which risk should the rep still explain before recommending them?

options.text: No currency risk, because a dollar quote fixes the dividend in dollars too
Currency risk on the dividend the company declares in euros
Home-country exposure is gone because the receipts trade on a U.S. exchange
She cannot sell until the French share certificates are shipped to her broker

explanation: A sponsored ADR trades in dollars, so the customer does not need a foreign brokerage account. The company still declares its dividend in euros, and the depositary converts that payment into dollars. A weaker euro means fewer dollars. The dollar quote does not remove that exchange-rate risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a dollar trading price with a dollar-fixed dividend. The issuer sets the dividend in euros, and conversion into dollars can change the cash the holder receives.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a U.S. listing as a substitute for the company's home market. The underlying business is still French, so country exposure remains along with the currency risk on the dividend.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes a shipment of the underlying certificates as a condition of sale. She can sell the ADR in the U.S. market. The risk to explain here is euro-to-dollar conversion of the dividend.

prompt: Before a 1-for-4 reverse split, a customer owns 200 shares of common stock purchased at $8 each. No fractional share is created, and she sells nothing. What position and per-share cost basis does she have after the split?

options.text: 800 shares with a $2 basis
200 shares with an $8 basis
50 shares with a $32 basis
50 shares with a $1,600 basis

explanation: A 1-for-4 reverse split divides the share count by 4: 200 / 4 = 50 shares. Total cost stays 200 × $8 = $1,600, so the per-share basis is $1,600 / 50 = $32, which is also $8 × 4. With no fractional share cashed out, the split itself is not a sale.

distractorExplanations.a: Runs a forward split instead. Multiplying 200 by 4 produces 800 shares and would cut the basis toward $2. A 1-for-4 reverse split reduces the count to 50 and raises basis to $32.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaves both the 200-share count and the $8 basis unchanged. Every 4 old shares become 1 new share, so the count and the per-share basis both change.
distractorExplanations.d: Gets the 50-share count but assigns the entire $1,600 of cost to each share. That $1,600 is the total basis, and $1,600 / 50 = $32 per share.

prompt: Helena owns 500 common shares that cost $22 each, a total basis of $11,000. The company distributes a 10% stock dividend to every holder and offers no cash alternative. She keeps the new shares and sells nothing. What is her per-share cost basis afterward, before any market move?

options.text: $19.80 on the original 500 shares
$22.00 per share
$24.20 per share
$20.00 per share

explanation: A 10% stock dividend adds 500 × 0.10 = 50 shares, so she holds 550. Total basis stays $11,000 because a pro-rata stock dividend with no cash alternative is not a sale. Per-share basis is $11,000 / 550 = $20. The same cost is spread over more shares.

distractorExplanations.a: Cuts 10% from the old price, $22 × 0.90 = $19.80, and keeps 500 shares. The company issued 50 new shares, so the same $11,000 is divided by 550, which is $20.
distractorExplanations.b: Keeps the original $22 basis. New shares were added, and the unchanged $11,000 is now spread over 550 shares at $20 each.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds 10% to the old price: $22 × 1.10 = $24.20. A stock dividend does not increase basis. Total basis stays $11,000, or $20 on each of 550 shares.

prompt: On a Thursday that is both the ex-dividend date and the record date, a listed common stock pays a $0.80 cash dividend. That morning a customer sells her shares regular way. Who is entitled to the $0.80?

options.text: The seller receives the $0.80
The buyer receives the $0.80
The buyer and the seller each receive $0.40
The sale cancels the $0.80 for this lot

explanation: Thursday is the ex-dividend date, and for this cash dividend that is also the record date. Her regular-way sale on Thursday settles on Friday, the next business day. She is still the owner of record on Thursday, so the full $0.80 is paid to her. The buyer settles too late to be on the books that day.

distractorExplanations.b: Gives the $0.80 to the buyer of a record-date sale. That purchase settles Friday, after the record date, so the buyer is not the owner of record for this dividend.
distractorExplanations.c: Splits the $0.80 into two payments of $0.40. One holder of record receives the dividend, and here that holder is the seller, whose sale has not settled.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a sale on the record date as a cancellation. The $0.80 is still paid, and it is paid to the seller who remains the owner of record that Thursday.

prompt: Two equity privileges are quoted for the same common stock, which trades at $37. The rights expire in 45 days and let holders subscribe at $30. The warrants expire in 5 years and are exercisable at $50. Which comparison should the rep give?

options.text: Both privileges have intrinsic value, because each allows a purchase of this common stock
Rights have $7 of intrinsic value; warrants have none today
Warrants are $13 below the market; rights are $7 above it
Neither privilege has intrinsic value until its printed expiration date

explanation: Intrinsic value compares the stock with the purchase price in the privilege. The rights subscribe at $30, and $37 − $30 = $7, so they have $7 of intrinsic value. The warrants exercise at $50, and $50 − $37 = $13, so they have no intrinsic value today. The extra years can support a market price for the warrant, but that price is not intrinsic value.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats any privilege to buy the stock as having intrinsic value. Only a purchase price below the $37 market has it. The warrant exercise price is $50, which is above the market.
distractorExplanations.c: Swaps the two results. The $7 gap, from $37 − $30, belongs to the rights. The warrants sit $13 above the market, $50 − $37, so they have no intrinsic value today.
distractorExplanations.d: Says intrinsic value waits for the expiration date. It is a price comparison that can be made now. The 45-day rights are $7 in value; the 5-year warrants are not.

prompt: Preferred shares with a $50 par pay a $3 annual dividend and currently trade at $40. A retiree wants the yield that compares this income with other preferred stocks using today's price. What is that current yield?

options.text: 3.0 percent
6.0 percent
7.5 percent
13.33 percent

explanation: Current yield is the annual dividend divided by the market price: $3 / $40 = 0.075, or 7.5 percent. Dividing by the $50 par instead would give the nominal yield, $3 / $50 = 6.0 percent, which is not the comparison she asked for on today's price.

distractorExplanations.a: Reads the $3 dividend as if it were already a 3.0 percent yield. The $3 has to be divided by the $40 price, which is 7.5 percent.
distractorExplanations.b: Divides the dividend by par: $3 / $50 = 6.0 percent. That is the nominal yield. Current yield uses the $40 market price, so $3 / $40 = 7.5 percent.
distractorExplanations.d: Inverts the division. $40 / $3 = 13.33, but current yield is income over price, $3 / $40 = 7.5 percent.

prompt: Every common holder receives the same 5% stock dividend, and the company offers no cash alternative. A customer has 200 shares in a taxable account, keeps the new shares, and sells nothing this year. How is she affected?

options.text: She owes tax this year on the 10 new shares and now holds 210
She owes no tax, and the share count stays 200
She owes tax as if the 5% had been cash, and she still holds 200
No tax this year, and she holds 210 shares

explanation: A pro-rata stock dividend with no cash choice is not taxed when received. She adds 200 × 0.05 = 10 shares and holds 210. Her total cost basis stays the same and is spread over those 210 shares. Tax on the position waits until she sells.

distractorExplanations.a: Taxes the 10 new shares this year. With no cash alternative and the same 5% paid to every holder, those shares are not income now. Basis is reallocated over 210 shares.
distractorExplanations.b: Gets the tax result right but freezes the count at 200. A 5% stock dividend adds 200 × 0.05 = 10 shares, so the holding becomes 210.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the stock dividend like a cash dividend and skips the new shares. She received stock, the count rises from 200 to 210, and there is no tax this year.

prompt: Tradeable rights sit unused in a customer's account. The subscription price is $18 and the common stock trades at $23. She says she will throw the notice away and do nothing before the rights expire. What should the rep recommend?

options.text: Sell the rights or subscribe before they expire
Throw the notice away, because a subscription price under the market makes the rights exercise themselves
Wait for the company to extend the deadline
Subscribe only if the $18 price rises above $23

explanation: The subscription price is $18, which is $23 − $18 = $5 below the market, so the rights have value. She can sell them or buy the new shares. If she lets them expire, she gives up that $5 advantage, and her percentage of the company falls when other holders subscribe. The company does not exercise the rights for her.

distractorExplanations.b: Assumes rights priced below the market exercise themselves. They do not. She must subscribe or sell. Expiration leaves the $5 gap, $23 minus $18, with the holders who act.
distractorExplanations.c: Expects the company to extend a valuable privilege. Rights die on the date in the offering. Waiting past that date wastes a subscription price that is $5 under the market.
distractorExplanations.d: Waits for the $18 subscription price to rise above $23. A price above the market would make the rights worthless. At $18 they are the valuable choice, $5 under the stock.

prompt: London ordinary shares change hands at 12 pounds each. One sponsored ADR represents 4 of those ordinary shares. The pound is quoted at $1.25, and fees are ignored. What dollar price for the ADR matches the ordinary shares?

options.text: A matching price of $15
A matching price of $60
A matching price of $48
A matching price of $3.75

explanation: The ADR bundles 4 ordinary shares: 4 × 12 = 48 pounds. At $1.25 per pound, 48 × 1.25 = $60. That dollar amount matches the underlying shares when fees are ignored. Converting a single share, 12 × 1.25 = $15, prices one ordinary share rather than the ADR.

distractorExplanations.a: Converts one share only: 12 × $1.25 = $15. The ADR represents 4 ordinary shares, so the pound amount is 48 before conversion, and 48 × 1.25 = $60.
distractorExplanations.c: Stops at 4 × 12 = 48 and labels those pounds as dollars. The quote is $1.25 per pound, so 48 × 1.25 = $60.
distractorExplanations.d: Divides after converting one share: $15 / 4 = $3.75. The 4-share ratio multiplies the ordinary price. It is not a second divisor. The ADR matches $60.

prompt: Sixty shares of a listed company closed at $90 just before the exchange applied a 3-for-2 split. At the adjusted open the market has not revalued the company. The customer who owns those shares asks what she holds and what the holding is worth. Which description is correct?

options.text: 40 shares at $135, worth $5,400
60 shares at $60, worth $3,600
90 shares at $60, worth $5,400
90 shares at $90, worth $8,100 because each new share keeps the old price

explanation: A 3-for-2 split multiplies the share count by 3/2 and the price by 2/3. She holds 60 × 3/2 = 90 shares. The adjusted price is $90 × 2/3 = $60. Value is unchanged: 60 × $90 = $5,400, and 90 × $60 = $5,400.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the ratio, turning 60 shares into 40 and the price into $135. A 3-for-2 split increases the count. Value would still be $5,400, but she holds 90 shares at $60.
distractorExplanations.b: Cuts the price to $60 and forgets the extra shares, so 60 × $60 = $3,600. The split adds shares: 60 × 3/2 = 90, and 90 × $60 returns the value to $5,400.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the shares and keeps the $90 price, which would raise value from $5,400 to $8,100. The price adjusts to $60 so that 90 × $60 stays $5,400.

prompt: On Thursday, June 11, 2026, a retail client buys an outstanding corporate debenture. The two sides did not agree to a cash trade. When does this regular-way corporate debt trade settle?

options.text: Friday, June 12, 2026, the next business day
Monday, June 15, 2026, two business days after the trade
Thursday, June 11, 2026, the same calendar day as the trade
Tuesday, June 16, 2026, three business days after the trade

explanation: Regular-way settlement for corporate debt is T+1, the next business day. A trade on Thursday, June 11, 2026, settles on Friday, June 12, 2026. Monday, June 15 is two business days later, and Tuesday, June 16 is three. Same-day settlement on June 11 would be a cash trade, which these parties did not agree to.

distractorExplanations.b: Counts two business days, to Monday, June 15. That is the retired T+2 corporate cycle. Regular-way corporate debt settles on the next business day.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses same-day settlement. A cash trade settles that day when both sides agree to it, and these parties did not. It is not the regular-way cycle.
distractorExplanations.d: Counts three business days, to Tuesday, June 16. Corporate debt does not settle on a T+3 cycle. Regular-way settlement is one business day.

prompt: One syndicate member takes a 10% share of an undivided Eastern account on a $10,000,000 municipal new issue. It sells its whole $1,000,000 allotment, yet $2,000,000 of the issue is still unsold when the account closes. What liability remains for this member?

options.text: No further liability, because selling the $1,000,000 allotment closed this member's share
$200,000, which is 10% of the $2,000,000 still unsold
$1,000,000, a second copy of the member's original bracket
$2,000,000, the entire unsold balance charged to each syndicate member

explanation: In an undivided Eastern account, each member remains liable for its percentage of any bonds still unsold, even after it has sold its own allotment. This member's share is 10%, and $2,000,000 is unsold, so 0.10 × $2,000,000 = $200,000. The $1,000,000 already sold was its original bracket, 0.10 × $10,000,000, and those sales do not erase the remaining liability. A divided Western account would have released the member once that $1,000,000 was sold.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes a divided Western account, where selling the member's own allotment ends its liability. This account is undivided, so liability on the unsold balance remains.
distractorExplanations.c: Restates the original $1,000,000 bracket, which was already sold. The open liability is 10% of what is still unsold, not another copy of the bracket.
distractorExplanations.d: Assigns the whole unsold balance to every member. Eastern liability is proportionate. This member owes its 10% share, not the entire $2,000,000.

prompt: Property in the city is assessed at $250,000, and the city levies 8 mills of ad valorem tax to support its general obligation bonds. The owner asks what that levy collects on this one parcel each year. What is the tax?
explanation: A mill is $1 of tax per $1,000 of assessed value, so 8 mills are $8 per $1,000. This parcel has $250,000 / $1,000 = 250 units, and 250 × $8 = $2,000. The same result is $250,000 × 0.008 = $2,000. That is the annual ad valorem tax this assessment contributes toward the city's general obligation pledge.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a mill as one ten-thousandth of value. $250,000 × 8 / 10,000 = $200. A mill is one-thousandth, so the factor is 0.008, not 0.0008.
distractorExplanations.b: Reads 8 mills as 8 percent. $250,000 × 0.08 = $20,000. Eight mills are 0.8 percent, which is $8 per $1,000 of assessed value.
distractorExplanations.d: Divides the assessment by 1,000 and stops at $250. That figure counts the thousands of assessed value. Each of those thousands is taxed $8.

prompt: Choosing for a taxable account, a client in the 24% federal bracket compares an in-state general obligation bond yielding 3.80% with a corporate debenture yielding 4.70%. She tells the rep to ignore state tax. Which bond leaves her with the higher after-tax yield?

options.text: The corporate debenture, because 4.70% is higher than 3.80% before any tax adjustment
The corporate debenture, because 4.70% times 0.24 leaves a 1.13% advantage over the GO bond
Either bond, because 3.80% divided by 0.24 produces a 15.83% equivalent neither bond pays
The GO bond, because its taxable-equivalent yield is 5.00%

explanation: Taxable-equivalent yield equals the municipal yield divided by (1 − the federal bracket). Here 3.80% / (1 − 0.24) = 3.80% / 0.76 = 5.00%. The corporate debenture yields 4.70%, which is less than 5.00%, so the general obligation bond wins on federal tax alone. The corporate bond's after-tax yield is 4.70% × 0.76 = 3.572%, below the 3.80% she keeps on the municipal bond.

distractorExplanations.a: Compares the raw coupons, 4.70% against 3.80%, as if the municipal interest were taxable. In the 24% bracket she stated, the tax-free 3.80% is worth more than a taxable 4.70%.
distractorExplanations.b: Multiplies the corporate yield by the bracket: 4.70% × 0.24 = 1.13%. That product is a slice of tax, not the after-tax yield, and it is not an advantage over the GO bond.
distractorExplanations.c: Divides the municipal yield by the bracket instead of by one minus the bracket. 3.80% / 0.24 = 15.83%, which is not a taxable-equivalent yield.

prompt: After buying a 5% municipal bond at 108, callable at par in 4 years and due in 15 years, a client asks which yield her confirmation will show. Which figure is disclosed, and why?

options.text: Yield to call, the lower figure on this premium bond
The 5% nominal yield, because a confirmation prints the coupon and ignores the dollar price
Current yield, about 4.63%, because the confirmation divides the annual coupon by the price
Yield to maturity, because the bond is confirmed to the 15-year date even though a par call is sooner

explanation: A quote of 108 is $1,080 per $1,000 bond, and the annual coupon is 5% × $1,000 = $50. On a premium bond callable at par, yield to call is lower than yield to maturity, and the municipal confirmation shows that lower yield. Approximate yield to call is [$50 − ($1,080 − $1,000) / 4] / [($1,080 + $1,000) / 2] = ($50 − $20) / $1,040 = $30 / $1,040 = 2.88%. To maturity, the $80 premium is spread over 15 years: $80 / 15 = $5.33, so ($50 − $5.33) / $1,040 = $44.67 / $1,040 ≈ 4.29%. Because 2.88% is lower than 4.29%, the confirmation shows yield to call.

distractorExplanations.b: Stops at the 5% coupon. Nominal yield is not the yield a municipal confirmation discloses when the bond is priced at a premium and can be called at par.
distractorExplanations.c: Computes current yield, $50 / $1,080 = 4.63%. Current yield ignores the premium the buyer will lose and the four-year call, so it is not the confirmation yield.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses the 15-year maturity. On this premium bond the par call produces the lower yield, about 2.88% versus about 4.29%, and the confirmation must show the lower one.

prompt: Retired and living on the checks, a client will place $1,000 in either a 5% GNMA pass-through or a 5% Treasury note. She wants a monthly payment, the full faith and credit of the United States, and she accepts that principal may return early. Which recommendation fits?

options.text: The Treasury note, because Treasury notes pay monthly and return principal when homeowners refinance
The GNMA pass-through, which pays monthly and carries full U.S. backing
The GNMA pass-through, because GNMA interest is exempt from federal income tax in the same way a municipal coupon is
Either one, because both pay twice a year and both return principal on a single stated maturity date

explanation: On $1,000 of face, a 5% coupon is $50 a year. A Treasury note pays that as two $25 installments and returns the $1,000 at maturity. A GNMA pass-through pays interest every month. The first month's interest on $1,000 is $50 / 12 = $4.17, and the check also includes principal as mortgages pay down. GNMA carries the full faith and credit of the United States, which matches her safety request, and she has accepted early principal. GNMA interest is taxable at the federal, state, and local levels; the fit is the monthly payment she asked for. Treasury interest is exempt from state tax, but the note does not pay monthly.

distractorExplanations.a: Assigns the monthly payment and the homeowner prepayment feature to the Treasury note. Treasury notes pay semiannually and are not prepaid when mortgagors refinance.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats GNMA interest as federally tax-exempt. GNMA interest is taxable at the federal, state, and local levels. The reason to choose it here is the monthly payment and the government backing.
distractorExplanations.d: Says both securities pay twice a year and lock principal to one maturity date. A GNMA pays monthly, and mortgage prepayments can return principal before the final stated maturity.

prompt: A water-revenue covenant requires net revenue of at least 1.25 times annual debt service. This year the system produced $4,500,000 of net revenue and owed $3,000,000 of principal and interest. Did the issuer satisfy the covenant?

options.text: No. Debt service divided by net revenue is 0.67 times, which is short of 1.25
No. Net revenue minus debt service is $1,500,000, and that dollar gap is not a 1.25 coverage ratio
Yes. Net revenue divided by debt service is 1.50 times, which is above 1.25
No. The covenant requires 1.25 times net revenue, or $5,625,000, and the system is short

explanation: Debt-service coverage is net revenue divided by annual debt service: $4,500,000 / $3,000,000 = 1.50. The covenant requires 1.25, and 1.50 is above 1.25, so the issuer met it. In dollars, 1.25 × $3,000,000 = $3,750,000 of net revenue is required, and the system produced $4,500,000.

distractorExplanations.a: Inverts the ratio. $3,000,000 / $4,500,000 = 0.67, which divides debt service by revenue. Coverage divides revenue by debt service and equals 1.50.
distractorExplanations.b: Subtracts instead of dividing. $4,500,000 − $3,000,000 = $1,500,000 of surplus dollars. The covenant is a 1.25 times test, and the ratio is 1.50, which passes.
distractorExplanations.d: Multiplies 1.25 by net revenue instead of by debt service. 1.25 × $4,500,000 = $5,625,000 is not the requirement. The requirement is 1.25 × $3,000,000 = $3,750,000, which was earned.

prompt: Only the homes along one newly paved street are charged an assessment, and those charges are the sole source of payment on the city's paving bonds. The city does not pledge its general taxing power. How should a rep describe these bonds to a homeowner who lives across town?

options.text: General obligation bonds secured by citywide property taxes, so her house is part of the pledge
Double-barreled bonds, because the street assessments and a citywide tax pledge both pay the debt
Moral obligation bonds, because the legislature is expected to appropriate funds if the assessments come up short
Special assessment bonds, paid by the homes on that street and not by her city taxes

explanation: Special assessment bonds are paid from charges on the property that benefits from the improvement, here the homes on the paved street. A homeowner across town is not assessed, and the city did not pledge its general tax power, so her taxes do not secure these bonds. A general obligation would reach citywide taxpayers. A double-barreled bond would add a tax pledge to the project source. A moral obligation bond would look to a legislative appropriation the government may decline to make.

distractorExplanations.a: Calls them general obligations secured by citywide property taxes. These paving bonds are paid from assessments on the paved street, and the city did not pledge its general tax.
distractorExplanations.b: Calls them double-barreled. A double-barreled bond adds the issuer's tax pledge to a project source. Here the general taxing power is not pledged.
distractorExplanations.c: Calls them moral obligation bonds. A moral obligation bond looks to a legislative appropriation that may be declined. Payment here comes from the street assessments.

prompt: Quoted on a discount basis, a 180-day Treasury bill with a $10,000 face amount is offered at a 4% discount yield. Using the bill convention of a 360-day year, what price does the customer pay?
explanation: The Treasury bill discount is face × discount yield × days / 360. That is $10,000 × 0.04 × (180 / 360) = $10,000 × 0.02 = $200. The customer pays face minus the discount: $10,000 − $200 = $9,800. The bill does not pay a separate coupon. If she holds it for 180 days she receives $10,000, and the $200 is the interest.

distractorExplanations.b: Takes 4% off the full face amount: $10,000 × 0.04 = $400, so the price is $9,600. The discount applies to the 180/360 fraction of the year, so the discount is $200, not $400.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds the $200 discount to par and gets $10,200. A bill is purchased below par. The buyer pays $10,000 minus the discount.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses a 365-day year in the discount formula. $10,000 × 0.04 × 180/365 = $197.26, and $10,000 − $197.26 = $9,802.74. Treasury bill discount prices use a 360-day year.

prompt: Displayed as 4.70 bid and 4.60 offered on a yield basis, a municipal serial bond is available from the dealer's inventory. A customer wants to buy it now. Which statement about the price she pays is correct?

options.text: She buys at a 4.70% yield, because a customer purchase is filled on the dealer's bid
She buys at a 4.60% yield, the dealer's offer and the higher dollar price
She buys at 4.65%, the average of the 4.70% bid and the 4.60% offer
The quote cannot be traded, because a lawful bid yield has to sit below the offered yield

explanation: On a yield quote, the higher yield is the lower dollar price. The dealer's bid of 4.70% is the yield at which the dealer will buy, and the offer of 4.60% is the yield at which the dealer will sell. The customer is buying, so she pays the offered side, a 4.60% basis. The spread is 4.70% − 4.60% = 0.10 percentage point, or 10 basis points. She does not buy at the bid, and she does not pay the midpoint (4.70% + 4.60%) / 2 = 4.65%.

distractorExplanations.a: Has the customer buy at the 4.70% bid. The bid is the dealer's buying yield. A customer who buys from the dealer pays the offered yield of 4.60%.
distractorExplanations.c: Averages the two yields: (4.70% + 4.60%) / 2 = 4.65%. The customer does not pay the midpoint. She buys at the dealer's offer.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a higher bid yield as a broken quote. On a yield quote the bid yield sits above the offered yield because the bid price is lower. That pattern is the normal one.

prompt: Inside her traditional IRA, a 54-year-old client asks to buy an in-state general obligation bond yielding 3.20% so the interest will be tax-free. A Treasury note of similar maturity yields 4.50%. She does not need withdrawals now. What should the rep recommend?
