Buy the municipal bond in the IRA, because the withdrawal of municipal coupons will be tax-free a second time
Buy the Treasury in the IRA; the municipal exemption is wasted in that account
Buy the municipal bond in the IRA if her federal bracket is low, since the exemption is worth more at a low rate

The general obligation bond yields 3.20% and the similar Treasury yields 4.50%. Using the GO bond in the IRA gives up 4.50% − 3.20% = 1.30 percentage points a year with no tax benefit in return. The rep should recommend the higher-yielding Treasury for the IRA. If she wants the municipal exemption, that bond belongs in a taxable account, where the 3.20% is federally tax-free. Her age, 54, does not change the account's tax treatment.

distractorExplanations.a: Keeps the municipal bond inside the IRA on the theory that the IRA shelters interest from a state or city. The IRA already defers tax, and the municipal exemption is wasted there while she gives up 1.30 points of yield.
distractorExplanations.b: Expects a second exemption when she withdraws. Traditional IRA withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income even when the coupon came from a municipal bond, so the exemption is never used.
distractorExplanations.d: Applies a low-bracket test. A low bracket makes a municipal exemption less valuable, not more, and inside the IRA the exemption is unused at any bracket. The yield gap is 4.50% − 3.20% = 1.30 points.

prompt: Security of titled aircraft matters most to a conservative buyer of airline debt. She wants the issue collateralized by that equipment and paid down in serial pieces, rather than a general promise of the company. Which instrument fits?

options.text: A subordinated debenture, which is paid ahead of the airline's senior creditors and needs no collateral

Commercial paper due in 270 days, carrying a lien on the same aircraft a trustee would hold
An equipment trust certificate, secured by the aircraft and retired serially

explanation: An equipment trust certificate is secured by specific equipment. A trustee holds title to the aircraft and leases it to the airline, and the lease payments service serial certificates that pay the issue down over time. That is the collateral and the paydown schedule she asked for. A subordinated debenture is an unsecured promise and sits behind senior creditors. An income bond pays interest if the airline has earnings and declares the coupon, so it is not dependable secured debt. Commercial paper is unsecured short-term paper. The 270-day figure is a registration exemption, not a lien on the planes.

distractorExplanations.a: Puts a subordinated debenture ahead of senior creditors and treats it as if collateral were unnecessary. A subordinated debenture is unsecured and is paid after senior creditors. She asked for equipment collateral.
distractorExplanations.b: Says an income bond must pay its coupon even when the airline earns nothing. An income bond pays interest if the issuer has the earnings and declares the payment, which is the wrong promise for this buyer.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats 270-day commercial paper as aircraft collateral. Commercial paper is an unsecured money-market instrument. The 270-day limit relates to a registration exemption, not to a lien on the planes.

prompt: Escrowed to its first call, a city bond will be redeemed at 102 in three years from Treasury securities held in escrow. The city is rated A. A buyer asks which credit and which redemption date now drive the bond. Which answer is right?

options.text: Price it to the three-year call at 102; the escrow, not the A rating, is the credit

Treat city tax collections as the source of payment, and use the escrow as a backup if the city later defaults

The escrow is built to redeem the bond at the call, here at 102 in three years. Per $1,000 of par, 102 means 1.02 × $1,000 = $1,020 on that call date, not $1,000 at the original maturity. The yield that matters is the yield to that call. Coupons stop at the redemption. The escrow does not keep paying to the old maturity date.

distractorExplanations.b: Keeps the city's A rating and the final maturity as the drivers. After the escrow is in place, payment comes from the escrowed Treasuries, and the bond is redeemed at the call rather than left to maturity.
distractorExplanations.c: Cancels the call and runs the coupons to the original maturity. The escrow is set up to pay the call price on the call date. Coupons do not continue past that redemption.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaves the city's taxes as the source of payment and treats the escrow as a backup. The escrow is the source that pays this prerefunded bond. The A-rated tax pledge is no longer what the buyer is relying on.

prompt: Predictable principal within a stated prepayment band is what a client wants from a collateralized mortgage obligation. She does not want the class that absorbs principal the other classes do not take. Which tranche should the rep recommend?

options.text: A companion tranche, because the support class is the one that keeps a fixed principal window
A planned amortization class, which follows its schedule inside the band
An interest-only strip, because that strip receives principal on a fixed schedule and pays no interest
An accrual Z-tranche, because it distributes a level principal payment starting in the first month

explanation: A planned amortization class is built to receive principal on a schedule as long as prepayments stay inside its band. The companion, or support, tranche takes the principal that falls outside that schedule, so its average life moves when homeowners refinance faster or slower. An interest-only strip receives interest rather than a fixed principal window, and faster prepayments shrink it. A Z-tranche accrues and waits. It does not pay a level principal amount from the first month. The class that matches her request is the planned amortization class.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives the fixed window to the companion tranche. Companions absorb the prepayment variation so the planned amortization class can keep its schedule. The companion's average life is the one that moves.
distractorExplanations.c: Assigns a fixed principal schedule to an interest-only strip. An interest-only strip receives interest, and heavy prepayments reduce the interest it will collect. It is not the stable principal class.
distractorExplanations.d: Has the Z-tranche paying level principal from the first month. A Z-tranche accrues and receives cash after earlier tranches are retired, so it does not start principal payments in month one.

prompt: Under the toll road's net revenue pledge, tolls this year are $9,000,000 and operating costs are $3,500,000. Annual bond debt service is $4,000,000. Which claim is paid before bondholders, and how much net revenue is left for debt service?

options.text: Bondholders first, from the entire $9,000,000, with operating costs paid from whatever tolls remain
The debt-service reserve first, so current principal and interest wait until another full year of debt service is set aside
Operating costs first, leaving $5,500,000, which covers the $4,000,000 debt service
The surplus fund first, with bondholders paid if the issuer appropriates the toll money that year

explanation: A net revenue pledge pays operating costs before debt service. Net revenue available for the bonds is $9,000,000 − $3,500,000 = $5,500,000. Debt service is $4,000,000, and $5,500,000 − $4,000,000 = $1,500,000 remains after the bond payment, so the debt service is covered. Bondholders do not stand in front of operations on a net pledge. That priority would be a gross revenue pledge. A reserve deposit and the surplus fund come after current debt service, not ahead of it.

distractorExplanations.a: Pays bondholders from gross tolls before operations. That order is a gross revenue pledge. This indenture is a net pledge, so operating costs of $3,500,000 are paid first.
distractorExplanations.b: Funds an extra year in the debt-service reserve before any current principal and interest. Current debt service is paid from net revenue ahead of a reserve top-up.
distractorExplanations.d: Requires an annual appropriation out of a surplus fund. Under this net pledge, bondholders are paid from net toll revenue after operations, which is $5,500,000 this year.

prompt: Two years after a par purchase, a 6% corporate bond trades at 90 because yields rose. The issuer has not changed the coupon. What are the bond's nominal yield and its current yield at the new price?

options.text: Nominal yield falls to 5.40%, and current yield stays at 6%, because the coupon was rewritten when the price fell to 90

Nominal yield rises above 6%, and current yield stays at 6%, because a lower price increases the stated coupon
Nominal yield stays 6%, and current yield is 6.67%

explanation: Nominal yield is the coupon rate, and a market price does not rewrite it. The bond still pays 6% × $1,000 = $60 a year, so the nominal yield stays 6% two years after the purchase. Current yield uses today's price. A quote of 90 is $900, and $60 / $900 = 0.0667, or 6.67%. The price fell because yields rose, which is why current yield is now above the coupon. Multiplying 6% by 0.90 to get 5.40% cuts the coupon and is not either yield.

distractorExplanations.a: Cuts the nominal yield to 5.40% by multiplying 6% by 0.90, and leaves current yield at 6%. The coupon stays 6%. The price change moves current yield, and 6% × 0.90 is neither of the two yields.
distractorExplanations.b: Sets both yields at 5.40%. Nominal yield remains the 6% coupon. Current yield is $60 / $900 = 6.67%, not 6% times the 90 price.
distractorExplanations.c: Raises the stated coupon because the price fell. The issuer did not change the coupon. A lower price raises current yield above 6%. It does not change nominal yield.

prompt: Including the school district overlap, a client wants this city's general obligation debt burden per resident. Net direct debt is $48,000,000, the city's share of school-district debt is $16,000,000, and the population is 80,000. What is total debt per capita?
explanation: Total debt for this comparison is net direct debt plus the overlapping school-district share: $48,000,000 + $16,000,000 = $64,000,000. Direct debt alone would be $48,000,000 / 80,000 = $600, and the school overlap alone would be $16,000,000 / 80,000 = $200. Both layers rest on the same residents, so the comparison uses the $800 total.

distractorExplanations.c: Counts the school-district share and drops the city's own debt. $16,000,000 / 80,000 = $200. Overlapping debt is added to net direct debt. It does not replace it.
distractorExplanations.d: Divides the $64,000,000 total by 40,000 people, half the stated population, and gets $1,600. The population given is 80,000, and $64,000,000 / 80,000 = $800.

prompt: Needing the money in 3 months, a client expects yields to rise and asks which debt holding best protects the principal she will receive on that date. Which recommendation fits her horizon?

options.text: A 30-year zero-coupon corporate bond, because the deep discount fixes what she will be paid if she sells in 3 months

distractorExplanations.c: Expects a premium municipal bond to rise in price when yields rise. Bond prices move opposite yields. A long premium bond would fall if her rate view is right, and it does not mature in 3 months.
distractorExplanations.d: Has homeowners prepaying faster because yields rose. Higher mortgage rates slow refinancings. Extension, not a rush of returned principal, is what a GNMA holder faces when rates rise.

prompt: Interest dates are March 1 and September 1 on a 5% corporate bond with $1,000 face. The customer buys one bond on Wednesday, April 15, 2026, and the trade settles regular way. How much accrued interest does the buyer pay the seller?
explanation: Corporate debt settles regular way on T+1, so a trade on Wednesday, April 15, 2026, settles on Thursday, April 16, 2026. Corporate accrued interest uses a 30/360 count from the prior coupon up to, but not including, settlement. March 1 to April 1 is 30 days, and April 1 through April 15 is 15 more days, for 30 + 15 = 45 days. The annual coupon is 5% × $1,000 = $50. Accrued interest is $50 × 45 / 360 = $6.25, which the buyer pays the seller.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops after the 30-day March count. $50 × 30 / 360 = $4.166..., which rounds to $4.17. Accrual also includes the 15 days from April 1 through April 15, and 30 + 15 = 45 days.
distractorExplanations.b: Charges the full semiannual coupon of $25. The buyer pays accrued interest for 45 days, not the entire half-year. $50 × 45 / 360 = $6.25, not $25.
distractorExplanations.c: Counts 60 days, two full 30-day months. $50 × 60 / 360 = $8.333..., which rounds to $8.33. Settlement is April 16, so April contributes 15 days, not a second full month.

prompt: PQR shares sit in a cash account at a $48 cost. The rep recommends a covered call: write 1 PQR Apr 50 call at 3 ($300). At expiration PQR is $56 and the call is exercised. What is the profit on the combined position?

A $300 loss equal to the call's $6 intrinsic minus the $3 premium, ignoring the stock sale

The short call's payoff is the $6 intrinsic ($600), which the writer gives up, so that payoff is not extra profit. The $300 premium is kept. Profit is $200 + $300 = $500. Marking the shares at 56 is an $800 price payoff. Adding the $300 premium makes $1,100, which still leaves out the short call's $600 payoff.

prompt: LMN was bought at $62, and the rep recommends a protective put: buy 1 LMN May 60 put at 4 ($400). At expiration LMN is $49 and the put is exercised. What is the combined result?

A $700 gain on the put after the premium, with the share decline left out of the result

distractorExplanations.c: Call versus put: this books the full stock drop and ignores the long put, as if the hedge were a call that pays nothing when the shares fall.

prompt: TUV looks only mildly higher from here. The rep recommends a bull call spread: buy 1 TUV Aug 40 call at 6 ($600) and sell 1 TUV Aug 45 call at 2 ($200). At expiration TUV is $52. What is the spread's profit?

prompt: WXY may jump or sink, and the direction is unknown. The rep recommends a long straddle: buy 1 WXY Sep 70 call at 4 ($400) and buy 1 WXY Sep 70 put at 3 ($300). At expiration WXY is $82. What is the straddle's profit?

prompt: MNO could break sharply either way before the release. The rep recommends a long straddle: buy 1 MNO Jul 80 call at 6 ($600) and buy 1 MNO Jul 80 put at 5 ($500). At expiration MNO is $64. What is the straddle's profit?

distractorExplanations.b: Call versus put: $5,500 is the stock's payoff with the put ignored, as if the hedge were a call that pays nothing on a decline.

prompt: UVW should stay above recent support. The rep recommends a bull put spread: sell 1 UVW Sep 45 put at 6 ($600) and buy 1 UVW Sep 40 put at 2 ($200). At expiration UVW is $47. What is the spread's profit?

distractorExplanations.d: Call versus put: the $400 was a credit on short puts, not a debit paid for calls. The puts expired, so the credit is profit.

prompt: XYZ is drifting lower, though a collapse looks unlikely. The rep recommends a bear put spread: buy 1 XYZ Jan 50 put at 6 ($600) and sell 1 XYZ Jan 45 put at 2 ($200). At expiration XYZ is $48. What is the spread's result?

distractorExplanations.c: Payoff versus profit: maximum profit is the 5-point width minus the $400 debit, or $100, and the payoff must be the full width. At 48 the payoff is $200.

prompt: CDE is priced for a quiet month, in the rep's view. The rep recommends a short straddle: sell 1 CDE Aug 55 call at 3 ($300) and sell 1 CDE Aug 55 put at 2 ($200). At expiration CDE is $63. What is the straddle's result?

prompt: Assignment is the likely ending on 100 FGH shares bought at $90. The rep recommends a covered call: write 1 FGH May 95 call at 4 ($400). At expiration FGH is $102 and the call is exercised. What is the combined profit?

A $900 profit

distractorExplanations.b: Payoff versus profit: $500 is the stock gain from 90 to the 95 strike, the capped price payoff. Profit still adds the $400 premium.
distractorExplanations.c: Payoff versus profit: $400 is the premium, the short call's credit. The long shares also gained 5 points up to the strike, so the profit is $900.

prompt: NOP shares cost $58, and the rep recommends a protective put: buy 1 NOP Mar 55 put at 3 ($300). At expiration NOP is $56 and the put expires worthless. What is the combined result?

A $200 gain on the put, treating the drop from the $58 cost as intrinsic below 55

The combined result is −$200 − $300 = a $500 loss. Maximum loss is (58 − 55) + 3 = $600, and it applies at or below 55. Breakeven is 58 + 3 = 61.

distractorExplanations.b: Payoff versus profit: $200 is the stock's price payoff. The long put's premium is still a $300 cost, so the loss is $500.

prompt: STU looked slightly bullish, nothing more. The rep recommends a bull call spread: buy 1 STU Jun 100 call at 9 ($900) and sell 1 STU Jun 110 call at 4 ($400). At expiration STU is $97. What is the spread's result?

A $500 profit that reads the net debit as a credit collected on a short spread

distractorExplanations.a: Payoff versus profit: the payoff is zero, but the $500 debit was paid. Profit is payoff minus that debit, so the result is a $500 loss.

prompt: HJK closes exactly on the common strike. The customer bought 1 HJK Oct 35 call at 4 ($400) and 1 HJK Oct 35 put at 3 ($300) after the rep recommended a long straddle. What is the result at expiration with HJK at $35?

A $700 profit, as if the straddle had been sold and both premiums kept

explanation: At 35 the call payoff is zero and the put payoff is zero. The debit was 4 + 3 = 7 points, or $700. Profit is payoff minus that debit: $0 − $700 = a $700 loss, which is the long straddle's maximum loss. A zero payoff is not a flat result, because both premiums were paid.

distractorExplanations.a: Payoff versus profit: both payoffs are zero at the 35 strike. The long straddle still loses the $700 debit, so profit is not zero.
distractorExplanations.b: Call versus put: $400 is the call premium. The put premium of $300 was paid as well, and the put's payoff is also zero.

prompt: A representative whose payout drops at the $50,000 Class A breakpoint has a customer with $50,000 ready to invest. The representative tells her to put in $48,000 and add the rest later, and does not mention the breakpoint. What is wrong with that recommendation?

options.text: It is a breakpoint sale that keeps her $2,000 below $50,000 and hides the discount
Nothing is wrong, because a representative is not allowed to say that investing the full $50,000 would reduce the sales charge
The fund may accept only $48,000, because an order that reaches the $50,000 breakpoint is rejected by the fund
She must sign a letter of intent and wait 13 months before any amount above $48,000 can count toward the breakpoint

explanation: She already has the $50,000, and $50,000 minus $48,000 is only $2,000. Under FINRA Rule 2341, sizing the order just below a breakpoint so the representative keeps a higher sales-charge payout, and not telling her the breakpoint exists, is a breakpoint sale. Investing the full $50,000 today would qualify for the reduced Class A charge. She does not have to wait 13 months, and the fund does not reject an order that hits the breakpoint.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the disclosure duty. The representative must tell her that $50,000 qualifies for the lower sales charge, not stay silent to preserve the higher payout.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the breakpoint as a ceiling the fund will refuse. A purchase that reaches $50,000 is accepted and is priced at the reduced sales charge.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a letter of intent with this order. She can invest the full $50,000 today. A letter of intent is for reaching a breakpoint with later purchases, and it does not require her to wait 13 months before today's dollars count.

prompt: Quoted at a $20.00 public offering price, an open-end income fund shows a NAV of $18.40. This purchase is below the first breakpoint, so the customer pays the $20.00 price. What sales-charge percent is included in that offering price?

options.text: About 8.70%, because the $1.60 difference is divided by the $18.40 NAV
8%, because $1.60 divided by the $20.00 offering price is 0.08
9%, because every computed sales charge has to be rounded up to the next whole percent of NAV
1.60%, because the dollar gap between the offering price and NAV is the percent by itself

explanation: The sales charge is quoted as a percent of the public offering price, not of NAV. Here the charge is $20.00 minus $18.40, which is $1.60. Then $1.60 divided by the $20.00 offering price equals 0.08, or 8%. Dividing that same $1.60 by the $18.40 NAV is about 8.70%, which describes the load as a percent of the amount invested, not the sales-charge percent. Nothing in the quote requires rounding 8% up to 9%.

distractorExplanations.a: Divides the $1.60 charge by the $18.40 NAV. That is about 8.70% of the amount invested. The sales-charge percent uses the $20.00 public offering price as the base.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a rounding rule. $1.60 divided by $20.00 is exactly 8%, and this quote is not rounded up to 9% of NAV.
distractorExplanations.d: Stops at the $1.60 dollar gap and calls that number the percent. The dollars must be divided by the $20.00 offering price to get 8%.

prompt: An equity subaccount inside a variable annuity falls 20% with the stock market. The insurer's general account, invested in bonds, does not fall. The owner has not annuitized and is alive, and the question is her current contract value, not a death claim. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The general account absorbs the drop, so her current contract value stays at the premiums she has paid
The separate account refunds the drop at year-end, because a variable annuity guarantees the assumed interest rate
The owner bears that 20% loss in the separate account
A state guaranty association replaces the 20% decline inside the equity subaccount while she is alive

explanation: Premiums allocated to the equity subaccount go into the separate account, and the contract owner bears that investment risk. A 20% market decline reduces her current contract value by 20%. The insurer's general account supports fixed options and insurance guarantees; it does not absorb a loss in a variable subaccount. The assumed interest rate is not a floor that refunds an accumulation-period loss, and a guaranty association does not restore separate-account market losses.

distractorExplanations.a: Assigns the equity loss to the general account. The general account did not fall, and it does not top her variable contract value back up to the premiums she paid.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats the assumed interest rate as a guaranteed refund during accumulation. The separate account does not repay a 20% market loss at year-end.
distractorExplanations.d: Expects a state guaranty association to replace the 20% separate-account decline. Those associations do not restore market losses in a variable subaccount.

prompt: Needing cash within the year, a 64-year-old customer has $40,000 as her only savings beyond a pension that already covers her bills. It becomes suitable once she signs the subscription agreement, because that signature is the suitability finding
She may need the $40,000 within a year, and the program is illiquid and can be lost in full

This non-traded exploratory program has no public market and can consume the entire $40,000. Under FINRA Rule 2310 that mismatch makes the recommendation unsuitable. Drilling deductions of a limited partner do not turn a pension into a reason to lock up the cash, and signing a subscription agreement does not prove suitability.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats intangible drilling costs as a deduction against her pension. A limited partner's tax items are passive, and the deduction does not cure the liquidity mismatch or the risk of losing the $40,000.
distractorExplanations.b: Imports an IRA early-withdrawal penalty that partnerships do not charge. Age 59 1/2 is not the test, and being 64 does not make an illiquid wildcat program suitable.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats her signature as a substitute for suitability. The subscription agreement does not erase a 1-year cash need or the chance of losing the entire $40,000.

prompt: Wanting a bond ladder that stays put, a customer asks for investment-grade municipal bonds that will not be traded when rates move and that will end on a stated date when the last bond matures. She does not want a manager swapping credits. Which of these fits?

An actively managed municipal bond fund whose manager agrees in a side letter never to trade a bond
A variable annuity fixed account, because that general-account option is a bond ladder ending on a date she picks
A closed-end municipal bond fund, because issuing the shares freezes the bonds until the last maturity
