prompt: During a fast market, a retail customer wants 2,000 shares of a thinly traded stock. She names a limit price, will accept a partial fill of any size at that price or better, and wants every unfilled share canceled at once instead of left working. Which instruction should the rep enter?

options.text: An immediate-or-cancel limit, keeping any partial and canceling the rest at once
A fill-or-kill limit, keeping any partial now and canceling only the leftover shares
An all-or-none limit, which may fill part of the 2,000 now and work the rest until the close
A plain day limit, so a partial may print now while every unfilled share keeps working until the close

explanation: An immediate-or-cancel order may fill any part of the 2,000 shares that is available at her limit or better, and it cancels the unfilled shares immediately. It does not remain on the book. That is the instruction that matches a partial fill plus an immediate cancel of the rest.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses fill-or-kill with immediate-or-cancel: fill-or-kill cancels the entire order if all 2,000 shares cannot be filled at once, so a partial is not kept.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses all-or-none with immediate-or-cancel: all-or-none forbids a partial fill and may rest, rather than taking any size and canceling the balance.
distractorExplanations.d: Mistakes a resting day limit for an immediate cancel: the unfilled shares would keep working until the close, which is the result she told the rep to avoid.

prompt: A customer who is short 400 GHI shares, with GHI trading at 36, wants protection if the price rises. She asks for an order that starts working only if GHI trades at 40 and then takes the next available price. Which order should the rep enter?

options.text: A buy limit at 40, which can execute only after a trade prints above 40
A buy stop at 40, which becomes a market order once a trade prints at or above 40
A sell stop at 40, which closes the short if GHI trades down through 36
A buy stop-limit with a stop of 40 and a limit of 36, which guarantees a fill no worse than 36

explanation: A short position is hurt by a rise, so the protective order is a buy stop above the market. With GHI at 36, a buy stop at 40 is triggered by a trade at or above 40 and then becomes a market order, which takes the next available price. That matches her instruction.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a buy limit with a buy stop: a buy limit at 40 is already marketable at 36, because she would buy at 40 or lower, so it would not wait for a rise.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses the wrong side: a sell stop would add to the short if the price fell, and it does not buy her in when GHI rises to 40.
distractorExplanations.d: Mistakes a stop-limit for a guaranteed fill: a stop-limit can fail to execute, and a limit of 36 would not carry out a protective buy after a rally through 40.

prompt: DEF shares are trading at 52 when a customer enters a sell stop-limit for 500 shares, stop 48 and limit 47. The next sales print at 50.40 and then at 45, with no trade in between. What happens to the order?

options.text: The 50.40 sale triggers it, and the shares are sold at the market near 50.40
Nothing is triggered, because the stock never printed a sale at exactly 48
The 45 sale triggers it, and the 47 limit leaves the order unfilled
The 45 sale triggers it and converts it to a market order, so the shares sell near 45

explanation: A sell stop-limit is triggered by a trade at or below the stop. The 50.40 print is still above 48, so the 45 print is the trigger. The order then becomes a limit to sell at 47 or higher. Because 45 is below 47, that limit is not filled, which is the risk of adding a limit to a stop.

distractorExplanations.a: Triggers too early: 50.40 is above the 48 stop, so that print neither elects the order nor sells the 500 shares.
distractorExplanations.b: Mistakenly requires an exact print at 48: a sell stop is also triggered when a trade goes through the stop, as the 45 sale does.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a stop-limit with a plain stop: after the trigger this order is a 47 limit, not a market order that can sell at 45.

prompt: Monday morning, a retail customer tells her rep to buy 300 shares of LMN today and to choose the time and the price. The rep does not buy before the close. On Tuesday LMN is cheaper. May the rep buy the 300 shares on the Monday instruction?

options.text: Yes. Naming the stock makes this a retail good-til-canceled not-held order that stays open until she cancels it
Yes. Oral time-and-price authority remains in force until the customer cancels it, so Tuesday's lower price may be used
No. Monday's order was already prohibited unless she had signed a discretionary authorization and a principal had accepted the account
No. Monday's authority ended at the close, so Tuesday needs a new order or a signed, dated written extension

explanation: The customer named the side, the 300 shares, and LMN, so the rep could choose only time and price during Monday without a discretionary authorization. Under FINRA Rule 3260 that authority ends with the business day unless the customer signs and dates a written extension. It does not carry into Tuesday, and the order ticket must show any time-and-price discretion that was used.

distractorExplanations.a: Misapplies the institutional exception: a retail customer's oral not-held instruction does not become a good-til-canceled order that survives the day.
distractorExplanations.b: Mistakenly leaves time-and-price discretion open until canceled: for this retail order it expired at the end of Monday.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses full discretion with same-day time and price: choosing only time and price on the day the customer named the security, side, and amount does not require a discretionary authorization.

prompt: A firm holds an open good-til-canceled order to buy 200 PQR shares at a limit of 40. PQR will pay a cash dividend of 0.50 per share, and the order is not marked do-not-reduce. How should that order read on the ex-dividend date?

options.text: Buy 200 shares at a limit of 39.50, and leave the share count unchanged
Buy 200 shares at the original limit of 40, because a cash dividend does not change this open order
Buy 400 shares at a limit of 20, with the cash dividend treated like a two-for-one split
Buy 200 shares at a limit of 40.50, after the dividend is added to the customer's price

explanation: On the ex-dividend date, FINRA Rule 5330 reduces this open buy limit by the 0.50 cash dividend, from 40 to 39.50, unless the order is marked do-not-reduce. The share count stays 200. A cash dividend does not multiply the shares, and orders above the market, such as sell limits and buy stops, are not reduced.

distractorExplanations.b: Skips the required reduction: an unmarked buy limit is reduced by the cash dividend, and do-not-reduce is the marking that would have kept the limit at 40.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a cash dividend with a stock split: the 0.50 dividend changes the 40 limit, not the 200-share size, and it does not create a 400-share order at 20.
distractorExplanations.d: Adjusts in the wrong direction: the limit is reduced by 0.50, to 39.50, not increased to 40.50.

prompt: A pending good-til-canceled sell limit sits on the firm's books when the issuer announces that those shares will undergo a 1-for-10 reverse split. Under FINRA Rule 5330, what must the firm do with that order?

options.text: Leave the limit price and the share count unchanged until the customer calls with a new instruction
Cancel the pending order, and do not rewrite its limit price or its share count
Multiply the limit price by 10 and reduce the shares to one-tenth so the order matches the reverse split
Divide the limit price by 10 and multiply the share count by 10, using ordinary forward-split math, then leave it working

explanation: FINRA Rule 5330 cancels a pending buy or sell order in a security that is the subject of a reverse split. The firm does not reprice this good-til-canceled sell limit or change its size for the 1-for-10 ratio. The customer must enter a new order if she still wants to sell after the reverse split.

distractorExplanations.a: Mistakenly keeps a stale order working: the rule requires the firm to cancel the pending order when the security undergoes a reverse split.
distractorExplanations.c: Applies split arithmetic the rule does not allow here: a 1-for-10 reverse split cancels the open order instead of rewriting price and size.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a reverse split with a forward split, and then adjusts an order that Rule 5330 says must be canceled.

prompt: The rep was told to buy 800 shares of HJK at the market. He mistakenly buys 800 shares of HJJ, and HJJ is lower by the time the error is found the next morning. How should the firm correct the order?

options.text: Leave the HJJ shares with the customer and rebill them at the next morning's lower price so she receives the benefit of the decline
Move the HJJ shares into the rep's personal account and let him pay the customer whatever loss she calculates
Book the HJJ shares to the firm error account at the original price, with principal approval, and enter the HJK order
Cancel the street-side trade without a record and wait to see whether the customer still wants HJK later in the week

explanation: The 800 HJJ shares were never the customer's order, so they go to the firm's error account at the original execution price. A principal approves and documents that correction, and the loss from the decline stays with the firm. The rep then enters the 800-share HJK order the customer actually gave, and does not park the error in a personal account.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives the customer a trade she did not order: the unwanted HJJ position is a firm error, not a purchase she can keep at a rewritten lower price.
distractorExplanations.b: Hides the error in the rep's personal account: the position belongs in the firm error account, and the rep does not settle the loss privately.
distractorExplanations.d: Drops the correction and the record: the firm books the error at the original price, a principal approves it, and the customer's HJK instruction still has to be entered.

prompt: Tuesday afternoon, a customer purchases a callable corporate bond in the secondary market at an agreed dollar price. No holiday interrupts the week, and the trade is regular way. Which handling matches the confirmation and settlement rules?

options.text: Settle on Thursday under a two-day corporate-bond cycle, and show the coupon rate instead of a yield
Settle on Wednesday, but omit any yield because a dollar-price trade discloses only the price paid
Settle on Wednesday and show yield to call alone, with no dollar price, because every callable bond is confirmed that way
Settle on Wednesday, and show the dollar price, yield to maturity, and that a call could change the yield

explanation: Regular-way corporate-debt trades settle T+1, so this Tuesday purchase settles on Wednesday. SEC Rule 10b-10 requires the confirmation at or before settlement. A dollar-price debt trade shows the dollar price and the yield to maturity, and a callable bond also carries a statement that redemption before maturity could affect that yield.

distractorExplanations.a: Invents a two-day corporate-bond cycle and substitutes the coupon for yield: this regular-way trade settles Wednesday, T+1, and the confirmation states yield to maturity.
distractorExplanations.b: Omits the yield Rule 10b-10 requires: a dollar-price debt confirmation states both the dollar price and yield to maturity, and the callable bond also needs the redemption statement.
distractorExplanations.c: Replaces the dollar-price disclosures with yield to call only: this trade was effected at a dollar price, so the confirmation shows that price and yield to maturity, not yield to call in their place.

prompt: Right after accepting a customer's order to buy an NMS stock, a firm that is not a market maker purchases the shares from another dealer at 20.00 and sells them to the customer at 20.30. What must the customer's confirmation disclose?

options.text: Principal capacity and the 0.30 difference between the customer's 20.30 price and the firm's purchase at 20.00
Agency capacity and a commission, because buying shares for a waiting customer is an agency trade even when the firm is in the middle
A single net price of 20.30, with no capacity and no price difference, because principal confirms never itemize a markup
The other dealer's name in place of the firm's capacity, because the contra party is the only required disclosure on this trade

explanation: The firm sold the shares to the customer from its own account after buying them at 20.00 to offset that sale, and it is not a market maker. Rule 10b-10 requires the confirmation to show principal capacity and the 0.30 difference between the 20.30 customer price and the firm's contemporaneous purchase price.

distractorExplanations.b: Mislabels a principal sale as agency: the firm took the other side of the customer's trade, so the disclosure is the 0.30 principal difference, not a commission.
distractorExplanations.c: Hides the offsetting difference: on this non-market-maker trade the confirmation cannot stop at the 20.30 net price; it must show the 0.30 difference and principal capacity.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes an agency-style contra-party disclosure for the required one: this confirmation must state principal capacity and the 0.30 price difference.

prompt: A message from the customer's own email address asks the firm to wire $85,000 of free credit today to a bank account the firm has never used. The message says she is in meetings, not to call, and lists a new mobile number. What should the rep do?

options.text: Send the $85,000 today because the message came from the email address already on the account
Hold the wire and verify the request by calling the phone number already on the account
Call only the new mobile number printed in the message, and send the $85,000 if the person who answers approves it
Wire part of the $85,000 today so the deadline is met, and verify the remaining balance after her meetings end

explanation: An emailed request to move $85,000 to a bank account the firm has never used, combined with a same-day rush and a request not to call, is a red flag under FINRA's guidance on compromised email. The rep holds the wire and verifies the instruction with the customer at the phone number already on the account, not at the number supplied in the message.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the sender address as proof: email from the address of record can be compromised, so the firm does not send the $85,000 before an out-of-band check.
distractorExplanations.c: Calls a number the request itself supplied: that call can reach an impostor, and it is not a substitute for the phone number already on the account.
distractorExplanations.d: Splits the transfer to dodge verification: urgency is a reason to hold the $85,000, not a reason to send part of it before the customer is reached on the number of record.

prompt: Once a customer signs paperwork at a new brokerage to move her entire account, that firm enters the instruction. The carrying firm disagrees with the cash balance and wants to block validation until she accepts its figure. What is required of the carrying firm?

options.text: Refuse validation until the customer signs a letter accepting the carrying firm's revised cash balance
Wait three business days before deciding whether to validate, and keep taking new orders in the account while it decides
Validate within one business day and transfer the cash and positions shown on its books
Reject the transfer, liquidate every position, and mail the customer a check rather than deliver the securities to the new firm

explanation: FINRA Rule 11870 requires the carrying firm to validate the account transfer or take a permitted exception within one business day. A dispute over the cash balance is not a basis for refusing validation. The firm transfers the cash and securities shown on its books and must complete that transfer within three business days after validation.

distractorExplanations.a: Blocks the move over a money-balance dispute: Rule 11870 does not allow the carrying firm to deny validation for that reason or to make the customer accept a revised figure first.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses the wrong deadline and keeps the account open for trading: validation is due within one business day, and the three-business-day period is the completion time after validation.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes a forced liquidation for the transfer the customer signed: the carrying firm delivers the account assets shown on its books rather than selling them and mailing a check.

prompt: The son of a customer calls, and the caller ID matches his name. He says his mother wants every equity position sold and the proceeds wired to his personal bank. He is the trusted contact, and no power of attorney is on file. What should the rep do?

options.text: Accept both instructions, because a trusted contact may order sales and wires for the customer whenever a relative calls
Enter the sales as unsolicited, then send the wire after the son emails his own letter of authorization
Sell the equities on the son's word and leave the cash in the account until the mother happens to call back
Refuse the sales and the wire, and reach the customer on the phone number already on file

explanation: A trusted contact is a person the firm may call about the account. That designation does not authorize him to enter sale orders or to direct a wire, and caller ID does not verify the instruction. With no power of attorney on file, the rep declines both requests and contacts the customer at the phone number already on the account.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the trusted contact as an agent: the designation lets the firm reach him, and it does not give him authority to sell the positions or wire the proceeds.
distractorExplanations.b: Accepts instructions from someone who cannot give them: marking the sales unsolicited, or taking the son's email as authorization, still leaves the orders and the wire unverified.
distractorExplanations.c: Carries out the sale before the customer has authorized it: neither the sell orders nor the wire can rest on the son's call when no power of attorney is on file.

prompt: Quoted at 24.10 bid and 24.18 ask, a stock is the subject of a customer's order to buy 600 shares at a limit of 24.50. She did not give the rep time-and-price discretion. How should the order be handled?

options.text: Route the 600 shares promptly as a marketable limit that cannot pay more than 24.50
Reject it, because a buy limit is valid only when the limit price is below the current bid
Hold it until a seller trades at the 24.10 bid, so the customer does not pay the 24.18 ask
Change it to a buy stop at 24.50 so it waits for a trade through 24.50 and can then pay more than her limit

explanation: A buy limit of 24.50 is at or above the 24.18 ask, so the order is marketable and should be routed for prompt execution. It may fill at 24.18 or any better price, and it cannot pay more than 24.50. The customer did not authorize the rep to hold it for time or price.

distractorExplanations.b: Rejects a valid marketable order: a buy limit may sit above the 24.10 bid, and at 24.50 it is executable against the 24.18 ask.
distractorExplanations.c: Holds a marketable order without time-and-price discretion: the rep should not wait for the 24.10 bid when the customer has already allowed a purchase up to 24.50.
distractorExplanations.d: Rewrites the instruction into a buy stop: that would wait for a trade at or above 24.50 and could then become a market order paying more than the 24.50 limit she set.

prompt: By late morning, a day order to buy 1,000 ABC shares at a limit of 18 has been filled for 350 shares at 18. The customer gives no new instruction. What happens to the unfilled shares?

options.text: The remaining 650 shares are canceled at once because the order was not completed in full
The remaining 650 shares stay open at 18 until the close, then expire if unfilled
The remaining 650 shares convert to a market order at noon so the original 1,000-share size is completed
The remaining 650 shares automatically become good-til-canceled at the same 18 limit and can work on later days

explanation: A day limit that is not immediate-or-cancel, fill-or-kill, or all-or-none may fill in part. The 350 shares executed at 18 are done, and the other 650 shares remain open at the 18 limit until the end of the day. If they are still unfilled at the close, that remainder expires and is not carried overnight.

distractorExplanations.a: Cancels the balance as though the order were fill-or-kill or all-or-none: this day limit allows the 350-share partial, and the other 650 shares keep working until the close.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a conversion the customer did not give: nothing turns the unfilled 650 shares into a market order, and the limit remains 18.
distractorExplanations.d: Extends a day order past its term: the unfilled 650 shares expire at the close rather than becoming a good-til-canceled order at 18.

prompt: A customer owns five XYZ call contracts and no XYZ shares, and he does not want to exercise. He tells the rep to sell 500 XYZ shares. How should the firm mark and accept that order?

options.text: Mark it long, because the five calls are the same position as 500 shares already owned
Mark it long and skip any locate, because a call holder may sell the underlying stock as a long sale before exercise
Mark the sale of the 500 shares short, and document a locate before accepting it
Mark it short exempt, because a customer who is long calls is excused from both the short-sale mark and the locate

explanation: The customer owns calls, not the 500 XYZ shares he wants to sell, and he will not exercise. Regulation SHO therefore requires the sale to be marked short. Before accepting it, the firm must borrow the shares, arrange to borrow them, or have reasonable grounds to believe they can be borrowed and document that locate.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the five calls as ownership of the stock: a long call is not the 500 shares, so the sale cannot be marked long while he refuses to exercise.
distractorExplanations.b: Skips the locate on the same mistaken long mark: without an exercise that will deliver shares, this is a short sale and the locate still has to be documented.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a short-exempt status for long calls: the order is a customer short sale, so it is marked short and still needs a locate.

prompt: Yesterday's confirmation shows a buy the customer says she never requested. She calls the rep that morning and then emails that the purchase was not authorized. What should the firm do?

options.text: Ask her to ratify the buy, because a confirmation that has already been sent cannot be questioned
Wait for a regulator to write the firm before anyone reviews the order ticket or speaks with her again
Move the shares into the rep's personal account if the position is showing a loss, and leave them with her if it is showing a gain
Investigate now, keep the email as a written complaint, and cancel the buy if she did not authorize it

explanation: The phone call requires an immediate check of the order ticket and the rep's instructions. The email alleges an unauthorized purchase, so it is a written customer complaint the firm must keep and handle under its complaint procedures. If the buy was not hers, the firm cancels it, restores the account, and bears any loss rather than asking her to accept the position.

distractorExplanations.a: Asks the customer to ratify a trade she says she never ordered: sending the confirmation does not cure an unauthorized purchase or end the duty to investigate.
distractorExplanations.b: Delays the review until a regulator writes: the firm investigates the disputed confirmation itself, and the customer's email is already a written complaint it must keep.
distractorExplanations.c: Parks the position with the rep or leaves a gain with the customer: an unauthorized buy is canceled and the account is restored, not sorted by whether the shares are up or down.
